articles.title: How a bank collapse left millions in limbo and toppled Paraguay's president
articles.summary: A bank's collapse in Paraguay left millions locked out of their money, toppled the president and exposed a web of political and financial ties.
body: ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — When Ueno Bank's services abruptly stopped working in the early hours of Tuesday morning, the consequences were immediate for the millions of Paraguayans who had come to depend on it for everyday transactions.

"People don't have any trust," said Elizabeth González, a 28-year-old barista at a café in downtown Asunción, a few blocks from Paraguay's Congress building, where protesters had begun gathering after the bank's collapse was announced Tuesday.
Earlier, one customer had walked into the café and insisted on paying in cash. He no longer trusted any bank.
"If Paraguayans themselves aren't confident right now, foreign investors will be less so," González said.

The collapse affected far more than the bank's shareholders. Ueno said it had 2.9 million customers — around 60% of Paraguay's adult population. The Central Bank said the bank had approximately 1.8 million depositors.
By Saturday, authorities said almost 1.2 million customers had received an advance payment under the state's deposit guarantee fund, but many were still waiting.
It also led to the impeachment and removal of President Santiago Peña, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and exposed a power struggle inside within the ruling Colorado Party.
The anger was palpable outside Congress on Friday, where hundreds had gathered to protest not only their inability to access their money but also what they saw as a broader failure of accountability.
"I came not because it affects me personally, but because it affects all of Paraguay," said Elodia Saveredo, a 71-year-old housewife who sells her own handicrafts online.

Batarram Caballero, a 23-year-old fifth-year biochemistry student and president of the student center at the National University of Asunción, said classmates had money frozen that they needed to cover basic expenses.

"It wasn't a lot of money, perhaps, but it was money for their bus fare. It was money for their food," she said. "To hear that and not be able to do anything because I don't have the resources to help them is very discouraging."

Ueno Bank launched as a fintech in 2021 and began operating as a bank in November 2023. Its meteoric rise to become one of the country's most important financial institutions was driven by slick marketing and a digital model based around convenience and cashback deals; customers could open accounts on their phones and were offered incentives to process payments through the platform.
Caballero believes the crisis was foretold by an intense campaign in the days before accounts were frozen.
"They were bombarding us with messages telling us to put our money there," she said. "There were also rumors about what was already on the cards."
The bank also held substantial public funds. The Social Security Institute, known as IPS, had around $355 million invested in Ueno, roughly 9% of its portfolio.
The sums involved have raised questions about how such a young bank came to hold so much public money.

Manuel Ferreira, an economist and former finance minister, told local outlet ABC Color that the collapse raised fundamental questions about how the bank managed its assets. He pointed out that, in a typical bank, shareholders provide only a small portion of the money behind its assets, while the bulk comes from customer deposits.
He also argued that marketing and discounts helped attract customers but did not create lasting assets. A bank's principal asset, he said, was its loan portfolio: money owed by borrowers.

But in the case of Ueno, many of those loans had gone to companies directly linked to the bank's controlling owners, Grupo Vásquez, including $146 million in loans made to just three companies. He described Ueno's promissory notes as being signed by the same people on both sides of some transactions.

The scandal hit Peña particularly hard because of his personal links to the bank's holding company, in which he held shares even after taking up the presidency. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno Bank, to head Paraguay's Central Bank in 2023.

In his asset declaration submitted weeks after taking up the presidency in 2023, Peña listed shares in Ueno Holding, then valued at around $845,000. Those shares represented around 1.6% of the company's paid-up capital when he later sold them in March 2025.
Prosecutors allege that, while president, he used his position to influence public agencies and state-owned entities to maintain deposits with the bank despite his connections to its parent group.

Peña resigned Thursday and was impeached and removed from office Friday. The following day, prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. He was ordered held in pretrial detention at a military facility pending the investigation. Peña has pleaded not guilty. Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, has been sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028.

Carvallo was also arrested and charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain and producing false public documents. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a police facility. Eight Ueno executives, including 36-year-old CEO Miguel Vásquez, were also arrested and charged.
The crisis has also put the spotlight on Horacio Cartes, a tobacco magnate and former president of Paraguay who wields considerable political and economic influence.

Cartes handpicked Peña, his former finance minister, to lead his Honor Colorado faction into the 2023 presidential election. But the relationship between the two men had become increasingly strained, apparently over Peña's efforts to establish his own power base within the party.
In September, senators aligned with Cartes sought information from the Central Bank about Ueno's transactions with related companies and its public-sector deposits.

After the bank collapsed, Cartes publicly distanced himself from Peña, releasing a public statement on Wednesday calling for an investigation and insisting there should be "no impunity for anyone." The following day, his faction backed Peña's impeachment.
The move was widely seen as a decisive withdrawal of political protection for Peña, and an opportunity for Cartes to reassert his influence.
But for those gathered outside Congress protesting, the scandal was about more than a bank collapse. It was a reckoning with Paraguay's political establishment.

For Rodrigo Piatti, a 45-year-old activist with the anti-corruption campaign group Comisión Escrache Ciudadano, the scandal would only lead to real change if the political establishment, including Cartes, were challenged.

"Everything that's wrong with Paraguay… is Horacio Cartes and his line of succession," Piatti said. "[Paraguay needs] the opposition to take power. A real opposition to take power, and for all these criminals to be put in prison. That's the dream of all Paraguayans."

The crisis has also raised questions about Paraguay's image among foreign businesspeople. Eduardo López, a 35-year-old exporter whose company operates in Paraguay and the United States, said the scandal would only worsen the lack of confidence he had already seen among American business contacts.
"We are a serious Paraguayan company, but [American businesspeople] don't trust the Paraguayan government," he said. "It's a disaster."
Nearby, Lizza Lugo, a 22-year-old student leader at the National University, expressed frustration with the status quo and said she hoped voters would bring change in the 2028 presidential election.

"The laws apply differently to those who have money and those who don't. That is the reality in Paraguay," she said. "I do hope people don't have short memories, because they forget these things very quickly."

articles.title: Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections
articles.summary: France says European officials will attend this week's U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, the first three-way round of negotiations since February.
body: European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.

"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.
The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.

Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.
On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.

This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.

Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.

Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.

For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.

The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.

Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."
The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.
Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.

Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.
And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.
Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."
In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

articles.title: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
articles.summary: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who will lead a caretaker government while negotiations take place, said: "I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks".
body: WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday's election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.

The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.

The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.

Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.

Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, "who won the election 2026" was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won't begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they've won.

With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.

Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.

Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.
Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.

Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.
"I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.
Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.

Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.

Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.
New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.

The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.

National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.

However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.
Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.

The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.

Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.
Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.
Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

articles.title: After a successful trip to Uruguay, Pope Leo heads to Argentina
articles.summary: On Sunday, tens of thousands packed the main square in Florida, Uruguay, to watch Pope Leo speak.
body: FLORIDA, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV wrapped up his visit to Uruguay on Sunday by praising the women who have passed the Catholic faith onto younger generations, as he highlighted the role the church has played since the founding of Latin America's most secular country.

Leo traveled to the city of Florida, north of Montevideo, to mark an important Catholic feast day before heading to Argentina for the second leg of his South American tour. It's expected to be the most politically delicate stop, given the Catholic Church's sharp criticisms of the austerity program of libertarian President Javier Milei.

For his final event in Uruguay, Leo celebrated the feast of the Virgin of the Thirty-three. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

Leo became the first pope in nearly four decades to visit Uruguay, in hopes of reminding its people that the Catholic Church is part of their very identity as a nation — even if, in subsequent decades, the country went on a deeply secular, and at times anticlerical, route.

In his homily, delivered in front of Florida's cathedral, Leo recalled the presence of the statue at the time of independence in reminding Uruguayans that "the history of peoples, too, cannot be fully understood without reference to God," and especially a mother.
He thanked all the mothers and grandmothers who have passed the faith onto younger generations, and acknowledged their pain when their efforts didn't stick.
"You taught your children to pray, and today they no longer do so. You used to attend Mass together, and it has been years since they entered a church," he said. But he urged them to not despair.
"Mothers and grandmothers: never tire of passing on the faith!"

Tens of thousands of people packed Florida's main square for the Mass under brilliant blue skies, some walking for several kilometers (miles) to reach the site. The city has a population of about 40,000 but the Vatican estimated 50,000 were on hand.

Fiama Pirez, an English professor, traveled from Montevideo for the Mass even though she could have seen Leo in the capital. She said she preferred a family outing to Florida so her mother could fulfill a dream to see a pope.
"I'm religious in my own way, and although I never strayed far from the Catholic faith, I'm rediscovering it today," she said.

In Buenos Aires, Milei is due to greet Leo at the airport before the two appear together for the traditional welcome ceremony and exchange of speeches. The Catholic Church has criticized Milei's austerity measures that have slashed social spending, and his embrace of artificial intelligence.

Milei has staked his presidency on cutting social spending to overhaul Argentina's troubled economy and deliver a long-elusive budget surplus. He has called social justice "an aberration" that amounts to stealing, and mocked as "huge stupidity" the increasingly common complaint in Argentina that families squeezed by his austerity program can't make it to the end of the month.

Leo, who took his name from the 19th-century pope whose encyclical on labor laid the foundation of Catholic social teaching, has made the poor and vulnerable a focus of his papacy, carrying on the legacy of his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis.

Posters reading "At last, a Lion who unites" appeared across Buenos Aires this weekend, a jab playing on the pope's name in Spanish — León, or lion — and the lion imagery Milei often uses to portray himself on social media.

"Argentina is a society currently experiencing significant upheaval, deep polarization, and an economic crisis, along with a president who defies conventional protocol — a leader who, at one point, even challenged Pope Francis," said Luis Bahamondes, a professor at the Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Chile.

Since taking office in December 2023, Milei has slashed Argentina's healthcare budget by 48% in real terms. Planned cuts to the public university system, which represents a near-universal point of pride in the crisis-prone country, sent students into the streets.
According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.

Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentina's troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.

Like Trump, Milei has also courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation. Leo has warned that the AI race poses threats to humanity and the environment and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.

Milei's government insists the papal trip is purely religious. "The pope belongs to all Argentines. He doesn't belong to a political party or a political camp," Karina Milei, the president's sister and secretary-general of the presidency, told reporters after a recent planning meeting for Leo's visit with church leaders.

In Argentina, Leo is completing unfinished business left by Francis. The Argentine Jesuit, the former archbishop of Buenos Aires, never returned home during his 12-year pontificate, confounding friends and foes alike.

"There's a lot of disagreement over Francis and his legacy in Argentina," said David Lantigua, a theology professor and faculty fellow at the University of Notre Dame's Kellogg Institute, which focuses especially on Latin American affairs.

Much of the polemics stems from his tenure in Buenos Aires, when the former Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio was a slum priest who advocated for the poorest and most marginalized — the sector of Argentines feeling Milei's social spending cuts the most.
"I think we'll see that kind of tension with Leo — that's the ministry Francis left behind," Lantigua said.

Leo, who spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru ministering to poor people, is very much a pastor in Francis' image and owes his pontificate to the late pope. But unlike Francis, he is returning home to Peru on the last leg of this trip, visiting a country where he spent two decades as a missionary.

Argentina's state intelligence agency said Saturday that a person had been arrested over death threats against Leo ahead of his arrival. A federal court in Campana, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) northwest of Buenos Aires, ordered the arrest less than 24 hours after the agency was tipped off, it said, without elaborating.

articles.title: Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: Comedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
body: Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.

On Thursday the one-time MTV host turned Christian and spiritual influencer was found guilty on three counts of sexual assault and one of rape, after a four-week trial that garnered massive media attention.
Brand had denied all charges and said he never had sex without consent.
After the jury handed down the verdict, Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand, 51, that he faced a "significant custodial term."

Danny Shaw, a crime commentator and former BBC correspondent, posted on X that while the maximum sentence for rape in the UK is life, 10 years is the average sentence, and Brand was likely to receive between four to 13 years of prison time.

The trial examined seven historic charges against Brand, brought forward by six different women. He was found guilty on four of the charges: for raping a woman who'd been to one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009. The locations of the sexual assaults were a bar, radio station and TV studio. Brand was also found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand's lawyer asked the judge on Thursday to grant his client bail so that he could spend the weekend with his three children, which the judge denied. Instead the one-time celebrity darling spent his first weekend in a prison cell in London.
He showed little emotion when the verdict was handed down, though his wife Laura — who has supported him throughout — quickly left the courtroom.
Many have called the verdict a significant milestone in the #MeToo movement, which has seen influential men held to account for using their power to abuse women.

Brand has also faced allegations of crimes in the United States. In 2023, a woman, named only as "Jane Doe," accused Brand of sexually assaulting her while she was working as a film extra during the making of the 2010 comedy movie "Arthur." That year, Brand married pop star Katy Perry, though the union lasted for just over a year before they divorced.

Addressing the media last week, London police detective Andy Furphy said that Brand had "used his influence, status and fame to prey on women — as his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

Camilla Long, a journalist for The Sunday Times — one of the first newspapers that investigated allegations of abuse against Brand — wrote in a column this weekend that "To sit in court 3 at Southwark crown court, hearing how Brand grabbed, pushed, groped and degraded his victims, was one of the most disgusting experiences of my life."
Long questioned how Brand got away with his behavior for so long, saying: "Never has a predator so loudly declared himself, yet been so roundly ignored."

articles.title: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
articles.summary: El Niño rains have transformed Chile's Atacama Desert into a spectacular sea of color, awakening a fleeting ecosystem of flowers and wildlife in one of the driest places on Earth.
body: COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.
This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.
Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.
But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.

The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.

More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.

Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.
"This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains," says Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park.
"But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."
Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.
Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.

Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.

Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.
This bloom occurs every few years in what is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth. But scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more frequent as changes in the climate bring unseasonal rains.
The phenomenon gives rise to a thriving, transient ecosystem, with insects hatching and attracting lizards and bats, as well as larger mammals such as the guanaco.
Biologists from INIA, Chile's national seed bank, are collecting specimens to analyze in their laboratory before the brief flowering season ends.
"It's very exciting," said Ana Sandoval as she delicately shook seeds free from their casings to take back to INIA's taxonomist at its base in northern Chile.

"It's as if the desert is awakening. Sometimes people think it's an empty, arid place, devoid of life, but actually our desert is just waiting for the right conditions, and any precipitation, to awaken it."
The seed bank wants to preserve the genetic material and unique adaptations each plant has developed to survive the extreme, arid conditions.
Sandoval points out different ways plants harvest water as she walks. Some leaves are covered in fine hairs; others have a thick waxy cuticle.
A national park dedicated to the desert bloom was created in June 2023 to protect a 141,000-acre area where flowers spring up every few years. Now local authorities want to go further.
Miguel Vargas, the governor of the Atacama region, is beginning the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the desert bloom phenomenon.

"This represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen special interest tourism and diversify our regional economy, which is currently heavily reliant on mining," he said. "Receiving UNESCO recognition would put the Atacama region on the world stage."
Vargas hopes this will become Chile's eighth World Heritage site within a couple of years.
This year, the bloom is projected to last until mid-November.

As the flowers begin to fade, scientists will be left with two tantalising questions: was this the Atacama Desert's largest flowering event on record, and might closer examination reveal any previously unknown species among the millions of plants?

articles.title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
articles.summary: At least six people were killed in the shooting, and three bodies of the suspect's family members were found at their home.
body: A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow and his parents and sister at their home has died in hospital, Polish police say.
The 24-year-old, who officials said was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies", was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
Krakow police said the suspected gunman died early on Monday morning.

After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man but did not confirm his name.

In the hours after the shooting, a minister said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.
People run for shelter as gunshots heard in Krakow
Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.
On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.

Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.
Speaking on Sunday, one of the two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.
The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers.
Watch: Doctor who treated victims of Krakow shooting speaks to the BBC
Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible."
"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."

Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.
On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.
Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded.
Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".
She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside.
Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".
"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.
In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.
After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków".

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.
Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

articles.title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
articles.summary: The BBC enters Marseille's dangerous underworld, where young people are trapped, brutalised and exploited.
body: Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBC
Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence
Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.
It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.
"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.
The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.
One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.
What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.

Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.

Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.
The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.
While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.
After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.
We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.

We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.
A still image from one of DZ Mafia's notorious video statements
The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.
DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.

The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.
Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.
In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.
France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.

The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.

Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.
DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.
We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.
They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.
And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.
Karine was called by a doctor about her son Hugo: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head"
Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.

Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.
But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.
"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."
Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."
Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.
DZ Mafia wields power in Marseille's Quartier Nord
Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.
Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.

Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.
"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.
It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.
"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."
Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.
Camil, who claims to have left DZ Mafia, only agreed to speak to the BBC away from the city - on a boat
Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.
In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.
Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.
The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.
"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.
"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."
Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."
DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.
He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.
"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."
During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
"Thank you, see you soon" reads graffiti on a wall, alongside price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana
We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.
He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.
"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.

articles.title: Trump says he was 'kidding' about Dana White press secretary offer
articles.summary: The president told the Ultimate Fighting Championship boss to "please take the job" in a Truth Social post on Saturday.
body: Trump initially asked the UFC boss to be press secretary on Saturday
US President Donald Trump has said he "was kidding" about asking Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be the White House press secretary.
Trump told the media on Sunday that White "loves the idea" but that the invitation was "just a little fun".
It comes after the president posted on his Truth Social platform on Saturday that he had offered White the role, asking him to take it while writing, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other."
White said later that day he was going to meet the president on Monday, but would not be drawn into whether or not he would take the vacant position.
On Sunday Trump told reporters White was visiting him on Monday for "other reasons".
"I think he's going to be in Washington. So he's going to come over and see me.
"I will tell you, I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana. He's great," the president said.
"But, it was it was just a little fun."
The press secretary role is yet to be filled after it became vacant in October when Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job.
She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest press secretary in US history and had held the role since Trump began his second term.
Trump's job offer came after a heavy loss in the midterm elections, where the Republican Party lost its majority in both houses of Congress.
In his Truth Social post on Saturday, he said he was "pleased to announce" that White "has been offered the job".
He said he had asked White to bring with him several current and former mixed martial arts fighters as "assistants".
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," he wrote.
Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference on Saturday, the UFC chief executive said he had "lot of jobs already".
"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he said of their planned Monday meeting, but did not say whether or not he would take the job.
White leads UFC, and PowerSlap , a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, as well as recently launching promotion company Zuffa Boxing.
He is also a board member of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
White appeared as a speaker in support of Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.
This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

articles.title: At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
articles.summary: The Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands remains dangerous for migrants seeking a better life
body: Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders estimates that 21 out of every 100 people who reach the Canary Islands by sea die during the crossing (file photo)
At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.
The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

articles.title: Pope delivers veiled rebuke of Milei's austerity measures
articles.summary: Pope Leo made the comments as he arrived in Argentina on the second leg of his Latin America tour.
body: Pope Leo XIV and President Javier Milei greet each other during the pope's visit to Argentina
Pope Leo XIV has said Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor, in a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.
The Pope was speaking as he arrived in Buenos Aires, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
In response, right-wing leader Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today".

This leg of the Pope's journey was expected be the most politically sensitive, with the president's agenda of slashing public spending having been denounced by the Catholic Church for hitting the poorest hardest.
"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," Pope Leo said.

He stressed the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs", and urged that "particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability" - a veiled reference to the government's controversial cuts to disability assistance.
In what appeared to be a rebuke of Milei's combative style and language, the Pope said strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words".
Milei had been particularly outspoken about Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, whom he called "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor.
On Sunday, however, Milei struck a conciliatory tone, calling Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history".
He was also keen to welcome the current Pope earlier, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy".

Pope Leo urged Argentina to safeguard its democracy. "Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community," he said.

In his own address welcoming Leo to Argentina, Milei defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of Argentina's constitution and of Western democracies.
The Argentine leader, who has said he will seek re-election next year, is a strong supporter of US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Pope Leo for his opposition to the Iran war.
Pope Leo's trip to Argentina has been described as a homage to Francis, who did not return to his homeland during his own papacy.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

articles.title: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
articles.summary: Two US fishermen say they spotted the man treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast.
body: The man identified himself as a pianist on the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship (file photo)
A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

articles.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
articles.summary: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.
body: Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
Uninjured passengers and passersby searched derailed carriages for injured people
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

articles.title: 'Devastating message' as ANC records worst-ever result in South Africa election
articles.summary: President Cyril Ramaphosa says the verdict must be respected, while the party's secretary-general calls the outcome "catastrophic".
body: Voters cast their ballots at a polling station during South Africa's local government elections in Johannesburg

South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".

While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 31% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 65% 20 years ago.

The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.

The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 25%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 10%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6%.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."

Entering the count centre on Sunday nigh, South Africa's president and ANC leader Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to be replaced as ANC leader next year

It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost its parliamentary majority in the national elections in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid in 1994. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is called the Government of National Unity (GNU).
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose only marginally from 22% in 2021, and was below the 27% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52%, an increase from 46% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.

"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC," said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."

The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."

The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline

"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."

The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.

South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.

"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is: 'Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together.'"
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

articles.title: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
articles.summary: Further details have emerged about two police officers hailed for preventing a Polish gunman from killing more.
body: One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague"undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.
The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six and injuring 15.
The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.
On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.
Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".
A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.
Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reported.
"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," Pędziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.
Pędziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.
"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who," he added.
Once the shooting stopped, Pędziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the perpetrator, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.
Mateusz Wierdak (left) and Michal Pędziwiatr treated the officers who stopped the Krakow attack
"He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt.
"If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance."
Meanwhile, Pędziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located.
"I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt.
According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.
The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański.
Investigations continued in central Krakow on Sunday before Main Market Square reopened
The attacker has not yet been named by authorities.
When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found.
The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.
Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.
James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square, external when the shooting happened.
The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".
Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.
Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".
Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there were multiple - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside.
How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded
Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".
He continued: "I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away."
The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views.
The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow.
Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.
The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.
The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city.
Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.
