articles.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
articles.summary: Jehovah's Witness leaders relaxed strict rules on blood transfusions, but the change came 23 days too late for Isaac Valdez.
body: Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure and his condition deteriorated rapidly
In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.

Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.
Jacob's "no blood" card which is like the one carried in Isaac's wallet

Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.

The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.

Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.
Jacob (right) believes his twin Isaac could still be alive if the change in teaching had come sooner

The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.

This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.

"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.
Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson Paul Gillies says the ban on transfusion of whole blood remains but blood components can now be used

We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.

He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.

But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.

Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.

It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.

And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.

He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.

Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.
"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."

With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.
More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.
It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.
Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.
Elisha Cummings was advised by an elder not to donate blood to her aunt Eva who died

They also cost her her marriage too, with her husband of 10 years leaving the faith and divorcing her after it came to light that he had had a blood transfusion as a child, something that was looked down upon in her Witness community.
"Since the blood policy change, I have not been myself," she says. "It left me in a sort of depressed mode."
"How many houses did I go to trying to convince people about the blood doctrine? And you're coming now and it's something totally different," Elisha says.
Elisha says her beliefs as a whole have been shaken, yet she feels reluctant to leave the faith, partly because it is what provides her with her community and she fears isolation.
In the past, those who disagreed with "blood doctrine" were ostracised or felt like they needed to leave the faith. Will they now be able to come back?
"Any individual that wants to come back to the faith is warmly welcomed," says Gillies, speaking of those who had left the faith because they had accepted a transfusion for themselves or a relative.
"If they would like to become one of Jehovah's Witnesses again and would like to speak to the elders, then they're very welcome to do so."

articles.title: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
articles.summary: From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes
body: In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.

Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.

“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.

From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.

Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.

Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.

The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.

Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.

Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.

“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.

It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.

That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.

Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.

It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.

In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.

Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”

A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Related: A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know it | Gordon Brown

Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.

It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.

In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.

In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.

In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.

The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.

Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.

As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.

Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

articles.title: Kraków shooting suspect who killed six has died, say police in Poland
articles.summary: Terrorism investigation was opened after a 24-year-old opened fire in a market square on the weekend
body: A gunman suspected of killing six people in a popular market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said early on Monday.

The suspect, a 24-year-old named in local media as Michal O, who authorities say was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been wounded in a shootout with police and had been in critical condition in hospital.
“We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Malopolska Policja wrote on X.

Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon, killing six including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours.

Karolina Galecka, an ⁠interior ministry spokeswoman, told radio TOK FM ​on ​Monday: “There ​were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted.
“These patches were ​associated with various motifs that ​are currently ‌being analysed ​by ​specialists,” she added, declining to comment further as the investigation was ongoing.
Related: Two police officers hailed as heroes for confronting Kraków gunman
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.
Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has deepened concern about extremism in Poland after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.
The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

The Kraków suspect drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.

articles.title: Monday briefing: Can we change the system that protects men like Russell Brand?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​Justice has been done for some of Russell Brand’s victims but the courts and the entertainment industry must do more to stop powerful men taking advantage of a culture that enables their behaviour
body: Good morning. Later today, Russell Brand will be sentenced at Southwark crown court in London after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others in separate incidents committed at the very height of his fame.
The trial judge has already warned Brand, a comedian and actor turned social activist then Christian influencer, to expect “a significant custodial term”.
The rape he will be sentenced for is one of the 9% of cases to make it from police report to court last year and, of those, one of 53% that result in a conviction.
Let that sit with you for a few moments: the justice done and the context in which justice is done.

Because the context around Brand’s offending is everything: the media circus, the tired tropes, the threats of litigation, the enablers and the institutional cultures of silence that protect powerful perpetrators. These all make it harder to expose predators and secure convictions.
For today’s newsletter, I spoke to senior reporter Emine Sinmaz and comedian Kate Smurthwaite about the trial and its aftershocks. But first the weekend’s headlines.

Poland | Six people were killed and 16 wounded after a gunman opened fire with a semiautomatic weapon in a busy market square in Kraków on Saturday, in what authorities are calling “an act of terror”.
Israeli elections | Israel’s president has picked Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, Benjamin Netanyahu’s ⁠strongest rival, to try to form a government, after a deadlocked election.

EU-UK | In a letter to Ursula von der Leyen, the leaders of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark have called for closer ties with Britain ahead of a crucial EU-UK summit this month.
Remembrance Sunday | Andy Burnham was joined by nine of his predecessors at the Cenotaph for what might be the last time second world war veterans outnumber former PMs at the service of remembrance.
US politics | Donald Trump set the stage for his administration to lurch further to the right this weekend, claiming the US had taken a “giant step back” by widely rejecting his party.

Woman One. Woman Two. Woman Three. Woman Four. Woman Five. Woman Six. We don’t know the names of Brand’s six accusers – sexual assault complainants are granted lifelong anonymity by the courts. But we know their courage.

The testimony of these women, connected only by their experiences of his abuse, laid bare what Guardian comedy writer Rachael Healy described to me as “the ultimate open secret”. Not all of them got the justice they sought: Brand was acquitted of two other rape charges and an attempted indecent assault.

Since the verdicts, police are bracing themselves for more accusers to come forward, with Brand now being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. Sources told the Guardian they fear the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”.

Having reported on rape trials and sat with survivors many times, I’d expected to feel more relief about last Thursday’s convictions. Perhaps it’s the echoes of those other women’s stories, especially those who didn’t get the outcome they wanted. Or the knowledge that a successful conviction doesn’t close the door on trauma. Or the weariness I heard from female friends this weekend at yet another powerful man, mainly protected by mainly other cowardly men.
Much was made of Brand’s comedy being “of its time”, steeped in Noughties lad culture. A decade hence, what will we look back and minimise as “of its time” in 2026? Non-fatal strangulation?

The trial was the culmination of a three-year inquiry by the Metropolitan police, launched in September 2023, two days after Brand was accused of rape, sexual assault and controlling and emotionally abusive behaviour by five women in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches, the Times and Sunday Times.

Indeed, Brand’s legal team tried to get the case thrown out before it began, arguing that he could not receive a fair trial because of the 2023 coverage. The judge dismissed this. Led by Ian Winter KC, the defence argued the investigations had “destroyed” Brand and “poisoned the well of justice”.
Following the verdicts, journalists witnessed Winter telling Rosamund Urwin, who led the investigation for the Sunday Times, “I hope you are pleased with yourself … You fucked it.”
He has since reported himself to his professional regulator.
Many more voices have praised the investigations as bolstering the argument for public interest journalism, at a time when it is increasingly under threat from litigious perpetrators.
The unprecedented media attention surrounding the trial gave the public a rare glimpse of the mechanics of rape prosecution.
Emine describes at least 20 journalists crammed into court 3 at Southwark crown court, with about 30 more spots in the overflow room and others watching the evidence online.

“Evidently not everyone was trained in UK media law, and they ended up crossing some legal lines,” Emine says. There was a moment of courtroom drama when the judge ordered the arrest of one of these bloggers, who had published identifying information about a victim. He was subsequently cautioned.

Jigsaw identification – different media outlets reporting details about a witness that, taken separately, are acceptable but when put together might indicate the individual’s identity – is a huge concern in heavily covered trials like this one and something Emine and colleagues were very conscious of. “As reporters, we all got together and discussed what we could and couldn’t say about each person.”
Another insight that may have shocked readers unfamiliar with such trials is how rape myths can be mobilised. “The cross-examination was uncomfortable and at times shocking,” Emine tells me.
Winter told jurors: “Not one of [the accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave” as Brand was attacking them. “Basically he was saying they hadn’t resisted enough”, says Emine.

Sexual violence campaigners tell me how disheartening it has been to see rape myths perpetuated, when there is substantial research to show that reactions to assault can be counterintuitive. There are many reasons why women may freeze or find they can’t move or speak, including the body’s automatic response to fear. Women can delay reporting in case of not being taken seriously or being worried about risking their job if they challenge a more powerful perpetrator that they work with.

In the aftermath of the case, Met commissioner Mark Rowley and prime minister Andy Burnham have said they will consider calls to impose a legal duty requiring judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths, one which exists in Scotland already.

Standup comedian Kate Smurthwaite was one of many women who spoke to Dispatches journalists about predatory behaviour by Brand and others. Since the #MeToo movement and high-profile cases like this one, she has seen incremental changes: more comedy green rooms signpost women to report predators to a designated person or offer to walk people to the station after the show. But she has doubts: “If the venue owner is obviously close friends with the man who has harassed you, is a piece of laminated A4 really going to protect you?”

Meanwhile, a section of the comedy circuit had reacted in the opposite direction. “Clubs boast that they champion “free speech” and welcome misogynist acts or performers making light of sexual violence. There are those who very loudly express support for Brand, Louis CK and others. If you’re the only woman on the bill, that can be intimidating”.

Meanwhile, there remain dozens of clubs and events that book “vanishingly small numbers of women”. Only when women are on half the bill and half the management in every comedy club, suggests Smurthwaite, will men “stop attacking us because they’ll be worried about the consequences for their careers”.

As the extent of Brand’s offending unfolded, so did the staggering degree of enabling that accompanied it: the staff who escorted victims to his home, the colleagues who laughed along to his humiliation of other female coworkers, the executives who didn’t want to lose their cash cow.

“Who’s going to hold those enablers to account?” asks Rachael Healy, who has reported on the extent of sexual harassment and abuse across the comedy and television sectors and gave evidence about it to the Commons earlier this year. “We’ve seen it from individuals around him, but also from large organisations like TV channels and comedy clubs.”

Since Brand’s conviction, culture secretary Lisa Nandy has called for it to serve as a “wake-up call” to the media world and beyond. Jack Bayles, a prominent TV producer who was said in evidence to have “laughed” as Brand sexually assaulted a woman has now “stepped back” from his current job.
The question now, says Rachael, “is how do we prevent the next Russell Brand, which is a question for everyone, especially the potential enablers”.

articles.title: Godzilla Minus Zero takes US box office by storm in opening weekend
articles.summary: The foreign-language film topped the North American box office with $31.6m in takings, generating $63m worldwide
body: Japan’s most recognisable film star shows no sign of losing its ability to captivate global audiences, after Godzilla Minus Zero – a foreign language film – swept to the top of the US box office on its opening weekend.

The film – the 39th in a franchise stretching back to 1954 – generated $63m worldwide, including $31.6m in the US and Canada, where it set a record for opening weekend receipts for the biggest live-action foreign-language film. It is shown in Japanese with English subtitles.
Filmgoers were just as enthralled in Japan, where the sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One set a domestic record for a live-action film, according to the Kyodo news agency.

In Godzilla Minus Zero, set in Japan in 1949 – two years after it lay “dead” at the bottom of the ocean – the creature resurfaced to respond to a new threat to the country’s attempts to rebuild after the second world war: a dragon-like beast called Ghidorah.
Related: Godzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streak

The film, directed by Takashi Yamazaki, shows a radioactively regenerated Godzilla confront its three-headed nemesis – which destroys buildings with lightning bolts fired from its mouth – with the help of human intervention.

“This historic opening shows how deeply audiences around the world connect with Godzilla and with Takashi Yamazaki’s vision,” Koji Ueda, president of Toho Global, which produced the film, said in a statement. “Our first near-simultaneous global release was built on that belief.”

In Japan, Godzilla earned ($5.75m) on its opening day on 3 November, setting a box office revenue record for the first day of a live-action release in the country and, according to Toho, more than double the opening day earnings generated by Godzilla Minus One.

Minus Zero qualifies as a live-action film as it was principally shot on-location, including at a sports park in Ibaraki, northeast of Tokyo, that was used for large crowd scenes and at a temple in Maizuru, Kyoto prefecture.
Industry experts said the success of its global release on Imax and regular screens worldwide had easily exceeded expectations.
“This weekend’s opening takes the Japanese production to a new level – it’s nearly three times the previous opening [of Godzilla Minus One] in December 2023,” industry analyst David A Gross wrote.

The latest Godzilla film faces competition from the Indian epic Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, which earned $55.7m on its opening weekend. The Hindi-language blockbuster – the most expensive Indian film ever made – made $8.7m in the US and $32m in India.

Godzilla Minus Zero and Ramayana were produced in the Imax format, with the former receiving an early Imax-only release last week. The large-format screens appear to have driven audience interest, generating 34% of Godzilla’s box office take on its opening weekend.
• This article was amended on 9 November 2026. Godzilla Minus One was released in 2023, not 2003 as an earlier version said.

articles.title: ‘I can’t bear it’: young family takes refuge in bedroom as choking haze engulfs Indonesian city
articles.summary: Mother tells of desperate efforts to keep her five-month-old son healthy as residents of Palangkaraya flock to clean-air ‘safe houses’ to escape toxic haze
body: Every day in Palangkaraya starts with an air quality check. For people who can afford one, a handheld device can test the air for toxic particles floating into their lungs. For others, a look out the window will reveal skies turned orange with smoke.
But for those closest to the fires ravaging this part of Indonesia, the check is done before they even open their eyes, with the acrid smell and the hacking cough that comes as they wake.

On the island of Borneo, people are facing life where the air itself is a threat. Windows are sealed with plastic sheeting, children are locked in bedrooms and families spend evenings inhaling oxygen from tanks.

At the centre of the crisis sits the city of Palangkaraya, home to about 300,000 residents, who have been besieged for months by wildfires engulfing its surrounding forests. Here, Apri Dona Yusmelita sits on the floor with her five-month-old son. She encourages him to take breaths from a nebuliser – a machine that will transport medicine to the infant’s tiny lungs. He has been sick for most of his short life.

“The cough is phlegmy, so he always has to vomit,” says Yusmelita, who also has a four-year-old. “So it’s like he struggles to catch up to his target weight. Because he’s constantly sick. So whatever he drinks, he vomits it all up, because he coughs so often.”

Since the fires started in July, Yusmelita has regularly had to keep her children in the bedroom where she has an air purifier. The 27-year-old moved the television from the living room to keep them occupied, but rotating power outages can make the days feel longer. Smoky air seeps into the rest of their home.

“Even eating had to be in the bedroom for the kids because their lungs are different from ours,” she says. “We moved everything here, especially when the smoke turned yellow yesterday … So it’s only safe in the bedroom.”

Over the past four months, her family has spent roughly half their time inside that single room. When her mother briefly took the children outside to play, their symptoms flared immediately. “I can’t bear it,” she says. “It’s so pitiful.”

Smoke from annual fires has become a way of life here. Many blazes were started intentionally using the “slash and burn” method of clearing land for crops such as palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.
This year has been exceptionally bad, with close to 2m hectares of forest and peatland burned in Indonesia. A “godzilla” El Niño has brought drier-than-usual conditions.

Authorities have been unable to cope with the scale of the catastrophe, meaning it is often local volunteers who monitor air pollution. The Ranu Welum Foundation, a local Indigenous organisation, has been fundraising for smoke “safe houses” equipped with air purifiers, oxygen tanks and nebulisers.

Roro Ardya Garini, 35, a co-founder, says they cater for vulnerable populations – the children and elderly – although on severe days anyone is welcome. “They come just to breathe,” she says. There are now 14 of these so-called haze shelters, often in rooms donated by churches or public buildings. The best ones have air-tight concrete walls and minimal ventilation.

The shelters are not a replacement for hospitals, Garini says, and sometimes volunteers have to send people away. Once, a baby arrived blue from acute oxygen deprivation and was quickly sent to the emergency room.

At another shelter operated by the volunteer group JPIC Kalimantan, Sabrina Alfiana supervises her four-year-old son, Fahreza Alfarizqia, as he inhales mist from a nebuliser. Air purifiers are lined up and plugged into the wall, as well as oxygen tanks.

Sabrina, 26, says she keeps her children inside, but sealing her home is a lost cause. “It’s smoke, right? Whether it seeps in through the cracks, the windows, you can still feel it,” she says. “Even inside the bedroom, we can smell the smoke.”
While Palangkaraya is on the frontline of the haze crisis, millions of people across south-east Asia have been breathing air that could be damaging their bodies in ways they cannot predict.

Thick smoke has drifted into Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, even reaching as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Schools have been closed, tens of thousands have been hospitalised with respiratory issues, and residents have been sharing images of rainwater turned black with ash.

In Singapore the government has set up its own air-conditioned haze shelters while Malaysia’s capital, Kuala Lumpur, has seen an uptick in pets brought to the vet. Toxic air has spiked demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say.
The Indonesian government has dispatched firefighters and says it will pursue the companies accused of arson, but decades of promises to address the fires have failed.

In Palangkaraya, volunteer Melodyna Adhesiva, 23, is in charge of taking air quality readings and posting the results on social media for the public. The readings monitor levels of PM2.5, particulate matter small enough to enter the bloodstream and cause lung damage.
The World Health Organization recommends a 24-hour average of 15 micrograms per cubic metre, and in Palangkaraya it regularly reaches 300. The worst reading Adhesiva took last month was above 3,000.

Her team has several devices, but the air quality is so bad they’re ineffective. “This one can only reach a maximum of 999,” she says, holding a monitor high up in her hand. “So we rarely use it for going out. We sometimes just use it for checking indoors.”

articles.title: New Zealand’s Opportunity party takes aim at populist politics as it prepares to enter parliament
articles.summary: Minor party leader Qiulae Wong says ‘populism doesn’t deliver results’ and that her vision for a low emissions future will drive its talks with major parties
body: A history-making centrist party that could influence New Zealand’s political direction has taken aim at populism as lawmakers arrived at parliament on Monday.

A nail-biting election failed to hand either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc a strong winning hand on Saturday. New Zealanders will now need to wait until 27 November for the final result, which includes the addition of about 400,000 “special votes” – those cast overseas or outside the voter’s electorate.

The Opportunity party, led by businesswoman Qiulae Wong, secured 5.9% of the party votes, clearing the hurdle to enter parliament, and becoming the first new party not born of an existing MP, or party, to enter parliament since the formation of New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996.
Related: New Zealand’s two major parties are flatlining as dispirited voters seek transformational change
Wong, who is of Chinese and European descent, also becomes the first leader of a party who has Asian ethnicity.
With the left and right blocs separated by just a few seats, after the official results are released, Opportunity could be in a position to decide who governs.

On Monday, newly elected lawmakers descended on Wellington for their induction into parliament, including Opportunity’s seven MPs. From parliament’s steps, Wong said it was “a huge day” for the party, whose nearly 150,000 supporters wanted a more pragmatic approach to politics.
“We’ve seen that populism doesn’t deliver results,” she said. “It is paper thin, it doesn’t have substance around taking countries forward. So it’s really encouraging to have had that support.”

Opportunity will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats, but its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.
“Ultimately, we need to align on that future vision for New Zealand,” Wong said.

Leader of the centre-right National party, Christopher Luxon, had previously ruled out working with Opportunity but he extended an olive branch on Monday. Speaking to RNZ, Luxon said he would call Wong “shortly” and discuss the need for cross-party collaboration.
“I intend to build a relationship with her and try and find common ground with her, too,” Luxon said.

National, and Labour – the centre-left mainstream party – experienced a near photo-finish on Saturday, with neither party clearing 30% of the vote. The two parties recorded their worst combined vote in MMP history.

In contrast, minor parties hoovered up support, amid public frustration with persistently high living costs and incrementalist policymaking. The Greens and Act both claimed their highest ever results, while New Zealand First jumped nearly 4% from its 2023 result. Te Pāti Māori also managed to retain five electorate seats, despite major challenges and in-fighting over the past year.

But while the minor parties celebrate their successes, New Zealand is reckoning with the aftermath of the messy election result, which is not only on track to deliver the second lowest voter turnout ever, but has triggered questions about the future of New Zealand’s voting system.

In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote. However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang. As it stands, New Zealand’s parliament could have an additional eleven overhang seats, because National and Te Pāti Māori gained more electorates than their share of the popular vote.
Political scientists say the complexities around overhang seats raise serious questions about MMP.
“It kind of starts to defeat the purpose of MMP,” says Dr Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, who edited a textbook on MMP.
Te Pāti Māori had campaigned for people to only give them their electorate vote, to engineer an overhang in the seven Māori electorates. So far, they’re on track for five seats.

Meanwhile, various right wing groups, including one backed by wealthy businessman Harry Mowbray, had asked supporters to party vote for the Act of NZ First parties, while backing National electorate MPs to engineer overhangs on the right. So far, National could have six overhang seats.
Greaves said such campaigns undermined the spirit of MMP, which New Zealanders voted for in the 1990s after a string of skewed results under the first past the post system.
“I am concerned these sorts of issues could create further polarisation,” Greaves said.
“The possibility is some people will be quite unsettled by this result … there might be questions as to the legitimacy of this whole parliament and this government.”
Additional reporting by Jamie Tahana

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: post war ‘security guarantees’ a key focus in upcoming Abu Dhabi talks, says Rubio
articles.summary: US secretary of state says some progress made on what security infrastructure could look like in Ukraine and Europe after the war. What we know on day 1,720
body: US secretary of state Marco Rubio said some progress had been made on what the “security infrastructure” of Ukraine and Europe could look like after the war with Russia, adding that talks this week could lead to further advances. Rubio’s comments on Sunday, ahead of his travel to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, come as Russia-Ukraine negotiations under US mediation have been set for Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump’s son-in-law, will represent the US in Abu Dhabi.

In an interview ‌with CBS’s “60 Minutes” broadcast on Sunday, Trump said he believed the war would end ‌soon and suggested Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered borders. “I think we’re gonna have it done, and I think it’s gonna happen and they’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine,” Trump said. Asked whether Russian president Vladimir Putin was stringing him along, Trump replied: “Oh, I don’t think so.”

On Sunday, Rubio said the whole time the US had been talking about Russia and Ukraine, “the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees” and what they would look like in Ukraine, and on the European continent. “I think that’s what the president’s alluding to – is that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture could look like post-conflict.”

French ⁠Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Europe would be well represented at the talks. “France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in ⁠these discussions,” Barrot told French radio station RTL. “I can’t ​tell you yet who will be ‌representing France on this ‌occasion, but France will certainly be there,” he added.

A Russian drone has struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine. Authorities say the attack on Sunday hit a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, previously targeted by Russian bombs. Ukraine said last Monday’s attack killed at least 55 people. No injuries were reported in Sunday’s strike but rescue equipment was damaged. About 50 people remain missing.

Power has been restored to the Russian-controlled ⁠Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine, hours after the plant lost its external electricity ⁠supply and had ⁠to ​use backup generators for reactor cooling, the UN’s nuclear watchdog said on Sunday. Zaporizhzhia, which does ⁠not produce electricity but needs power supplied by two external links to keep nuclear fuel cool, lost ⁠its off-site electricity supply earlier on Sunday after the Ferosplavna power ​line disconnected. The International Atomic ‌Energy Agency said the cause and location of the disconnection were unknown. The loss of power was the plant’s 27th such incident since the beginning of the conflict.

Russia said ⁠on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels ⁠that were carrying military ⁠goods ​for Ukraine and two electricity substations, which it said supplied power to ⁠the Ukrainian defence industry, Reuters reports. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering ⁠weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea ​port of Odesa, ‌and another in ‌the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same ‌southwestern region of Ukraine. According to the ministry, the second container ship had delivered dual-use cargo to Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, ‌was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.

Moldova on Sunday launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid, to reduce its reliance on Russian energy. “For decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us,” President Maia Sandu wrote on X. “No more. Moldova buys zero Russian gas.” Achieving energy security is a priority for the former Soviet republic of 2.6 million people, which has faced difficulties since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Tony Abbott calls Julia Gillard’s famous misogyny speech ‘over the top’ and ‘unjustified’
articles.summary: ABC program takes Australians back to 9 October 2012, the day the prime minister told Tony Abbott she would ‘not be lectured about sexism’
body: “For fuck’s sake,” Julia Gillard says.
Australia’s first female prime minister is recalling Tuesday 9 October 2012 – the day she delivered her famous misogyny speech.
Gillard, her adversary at the time, Tony Abbott, and others who were there have relived it for an episode of I Was Actually There, to be aired by the ABC on Monday night.
As it went viral – and global – it became a rallying cry for women and an unforgettable moment in Australian political history, and television history.
Speaking on the program, Abbott recalled his relationship with Gillard – one of mutual respect – had deteriorated prior to the speech.
“I thought it was a pretty over the top and unjustified attack,” he said.
“Gillard trotted out a whole lot of things where I was regarded as having acted in, I guess, an old-fashioned, ham-fisted, insensitive way.
Related: ‘It took on a life of its own’: the story behind Julia Gillard’s misogyny speech
“But again, I think most of those accusations were either over the top or slightly unfair.”
At the time, many in the press gallery and parliament saw the speech as Gillard’s attempt to distract from a scandal engulfing speaker Peter Slipper and threatening Labor’s hold on power.
Gillard’s government was in minority and reliant on independents to pass new legislation. Every vote was critical.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Slipper had quit the Liberal party to take up the speakership, removing himself from that side of the ledger, but it remained a precarious time for the government.
And Abbott was keen to savage Gillard on the Slipper issue, which was dominating the headlines on 9 October.
“He was essentially a Liberal party turncoat put into the speakership because Julia Gillard was desperate to prop up her numbers,” Abbott says.
Slipper had been accused of sexually harassing a staffer, James Ashby, who went on to become Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man and is now the party director of One Nation.

The court proceedings revealed texts from Slipper in which he likened female genitalia to molluscs. Slipper denied the allegations, and they were struck out in 2012. Ashby challenged the findings in the federal court and won the appeal against that decision but later dropped the case.
Gillard’s office knew the opposition would weaponise the issue, particularly its sexist nature.
The irony, Gillard says, was that Abbott was “almost … rent-a-gaffe about sexism issues”.
He famously referred to what “the housewives of Australia” needed to understand about climate change, and stood in front of “ditch the witch” and “Bob Brown’s bitch” signs at a protest.
“I always thought, you know, in the early days of my prime ministership that I didn’t need to answer the gendered critiques because over time they would fall away,” Gillard says on the program.

“And here I was two years later, and it was as bad as it had ever been, if not worse. Now all of this was going to be weirdly spun against me, that now I was going to be the one who was, you know, sort of skewered on this sexism critique.
“There was a phrase going through my head. That phrase, unpleasantly, was: ‘For fuck’s sake, like, how did we end up here?’”
So she and her staffers gathered some of Abbott’s “greatest hits” for a potential response. That handful of quotes would eventually become part of the otherwise unscripted speech.
She describes the adrenaline kicking in as she approached the chamber for question time.
Abbott stood up, and called for a vote to sack Slipper over the text messages.
The prime minister wouldn’t usually reply for the government during such “shenanigans”, Gillard says.
But in his motion, Abbott said the government should have “died of shame”, an echo of a phrase used by shock jock Alan Jones.
Jones, now on trial for charges of indecent assault and sexual touching (which he denies and has pleaded not guilty), had said after Gillard’s father died that he had “died of shame”.
Related: Julia Gillard’s misogyny speech voted ‘most unforgettable’ moment in Australian TV history
Abbott is still unrepentant about the remarks, describing them as “a bit of niggle”.
“I think it was reasonable of me to say that it was a government that should be a little bit ashamed of itself,” he says.
“Given that, I say, I am not conscious of ever treating women differently simply by virtue of them being women, I certainly am not conscious of ever having treated women in a lesser way.”
Slipper’s resignation as speaker the next day was a vindication of his position, he says.
Abbott using that same phrase spurred Gillard into action.
She felt “a kind of cool anger”, she says, as she rose to speak.
“I will not be lectured about sexism and misogyny by this man. I will not,” she told parliament in response.
“And the government will not be lectured about sexism and misogyny by this man.

articles.title: Two police officers hailed as heroes for confronting Kraków gunman
articles.summary: Jakub Kulik critically injured and Artur Morański also wounded after actions that ‘prevented further casualties’
body: Two Polish police officers who were injured as they pursued and detained the gunman in Kraków on Saturday have been hailed as heroes.

One of them is Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, who was left critically injured after a close-range exchange of fire with the suspect, a 24-year-old Polish national who killed six and injured 17 in an attack believed to have been inspired by far-right ideologies.
The other injured police officer is Artur Morański. Both are under 30 years old, the Polish news network TVP World reported.
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said on Saturday in a post on X: “They probably saved many human lives, disregarding the risk to their own.”
The Polish justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said the rapid response and heroism of the two police officers “prevented further human casualties”.
Police arrived at the scene 23 seconds after receiving the first emergency call from Kraków’s main square, where the suspect was shooting at random from his car.

Footage that emerged on Sunday showed two police officers exchanging fire with the gunman. One of the officers then apprehended the suspect on the ground before firing his own weapon several times. The officer then fell down, apparently injured himself.
Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, stepped in to help.
Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help”, Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet.
“Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”
Kulik, from the southern Polish city of Bielsko-Biala, was hit by three bullets and underwent surgery on Saturday. There has been a national appeal for blood donors.
Morański was shot in the chest area and also underwent surgery. Both men were brought out of medically induced comas on Sunday, Polskie Radio 24 reported.

Kulik is also a member of the volunteer fire service in Bielsko-Biala. “We’re very proud of him,” a volunteer firefighter from the city’s Leszczyny district told the local news website Bielsko.biala.pl. “He responds to emergencies just like we do.”

TVP World reported that Morański was from Powroźnik, a village about 90 miles (150km) south-east of Krakow and close to the border with Slovakia. A mass was held for him at the local church on Sunday.

articles.title: Gadi Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu allies as he strives to form government
articles.summary: Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’
body: Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis.

Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.

“We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the state of Israel,” said Eisenkot, who had traded his usual all black for a suit and tie at a ceremony at the presidential office. “We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps.”

Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.
Eisenkot and Herzog acknowledged Israel’s growing isolation under Netanyahu, who is wanted by the international criminal court.

In the US, Israel’s closest ally, Democrats on Tuesday swept the midterm elections, with calls to rein in Israel after the devastation in Gaza and the unpopular Iran war, which Netanyahu launched with Donald Trump.
Eisenkot said: “We are in the midst of a devastating diplomatic crisis. Even our closest friends and strategic allies are saying their relationship with Israel must be reassessed.”
He appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud party as well as the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to join him – but only with himself as prime minister.
“My door is open and my hand is extended, wholeheartedly and willingly, to anyone who understands the gravity of this moment,” he said.
Related: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in the October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.

Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, has already said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.
Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.
Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.

Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement. These types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse.
Related: Donald Trump’s power is on the wane. What next for Russia, Israel – and the rest of us? | Simon Tisdall
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and has vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.

Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.
If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.

articles.title: Israel’s president picks Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form government
articles.summary: Knesset has been deadlocked since the election last month when Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority
body: Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, the prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ⁠strongest rival, to ⁠try to ​form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man ⁠with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.
Related: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
Netanyahu ‌is fighting to hold on to office ‌after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc ‌in parliament.
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, 66-year-old Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.

Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of Eisenkot’s partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.
Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.
Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.

Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement; these types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse.
Related: Donald Trump’s power is on the wane. What next for Russia, Israel – and the rest of us? | Simon Tisdall
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
But he opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.

Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.
If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.

articles.title: Polish prosecutors open terrorism investigation into Kraków shooting
articles.summary: Six people killed in attack probably inspired by far right, according to officials, as police say suspect’s parents and sister found dead at his home
body: Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation after a 24-year-old man opened fire in a busy market square in Kraków, killing six people including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that authorities said was probably inspired by far-right ideologies.
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack on Saturday afternoon were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.

The Kraków suspect, a Polish national named in local media as Michal O, drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect, who was apprehended and taken to hospital after being wounded in an exchange of fire with police, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

Four women and two men were killed, including a British citizen, Polish police said. Three of the victims were Polish women. Krzysztof Klęczar, a regional official, said on Sunday that a 51-year-old Austrian woman had also been killed and the British victim was a 32-year-old man.
Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.
Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition. The suspect underwent surgery in hospital, where he was under heavy police guard.

The bodies of the suspect’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.

Mourners left candles in tribute to victims in the square, which was still partially cordoned off on Sunday. Flags across the country were lowered to half mast, as were European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

The Polish defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, called the shooting an “act of terror” against the people of Kraków, Poland’s second largest city, which receives 15 million visitors a year, most of them passing through the main square.

Kraków authorities said the square and adjoining streets “as well as sections along the perpetrator’s escape route” would be closed for several hours. Police in Warsaw, the Polish capital, said security had been bolstered there.

Maria, a 20-year-old employee at a cafe in Warsaw, told Reuters she “almost burst into tears” when she heard about the attack in Kraków. “Recent events – not just this one, but things happening lately – are really affecting our sense of security,” ⁠she said.
The daily newspaper Rzeczpospolita said in an editorial that the mass shooting had brought a “brutal end ​to an era in which Poland was ​considered an island of safety”.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “I’m shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today. My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said his country stood in solidarity with its neighbour, calling the shooting a shocking crime.

France’s Emmanuel Macron described “shock and disbelief following the tragic shooting in Kraków”, while the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said: “The events in Kraków have deeply affected me,” adding that Germany stood with Poland “as a friend and partner in these difficult times”.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, expressed condolences to Poland “following the vile and unacceptable act of violence”.

articles.title: Election results in Brazil, Serbia, Israel and US renew faith in resilience of democracy
articles.summary: Four pivotal elections in past two weeks show power of grassroots activism to push back against authoritarianism
body: A sequence of four pivotal elections over the past two weeks in disparate regions of the world has inflicted significant setbacks on authoritarian leaders, and inspired renewed faith that democracy is more resilient than had been feared.
Related: Ten days that could shake the world: democratic norms at stake in four pivotal elections

The elections in Brazil, Serbia, Israel and the US were held in widely varying circumstances with unique factors, but each showed the power of grassroots activism to produce surprises that pushed back against would-be autocrats and could perhaps begin to reverse a worldwide drift towards authoritarianism.

In Brazil, a surge in turnout in the second round of presidential elections on 25 October, fuelled by grassroots activism and the canny use of social media, stopped a far-right authoritarian movement consolidating its grip on the country, three weeks after it won control of Congress and established a strong lead in the contest for the presidency.

On the same day, thousands of miles away in Serbia, a grassroots movement led by students inflicted a shock defeat on a regime which had entrenched its hold on power over the preceding 14 years with a relentless violation of democratic norms. The margin of victory was sufficient to dispel any thoughts the outgoing leader Aleksandar Vučić may have had of trying to annul the result by force.

Elections two days later in Israel were far less clearcut. Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister who has dominated Israeli politics over the past three decades, lost his majority in a rebuke to his attempts to politicise state security agencies and infringe the independence of the press and judiciary.

The mainstream Jewish opposition parties seeking to oust Netanyahu are keen to restore those democratic norms, but more than 10 days after the election it is unclear how far they are prepared to go in cooperating with Arab Israeli parties in order to form a government.

The surge in support for these parties, boosted by a doubling in turnout of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, was the greatest surprise of the elections. Netanyahu is, however, seeking to delegitimise their success with claims – unsupported by evidence – of foreign funding and vote buying, while Jewish opposition leaders remain reluctant to collaboration across Israel’s ethnic divide.

The trajectory in all three is bound to be affected by the outcome of the fourth election in this 10-day sequence. The sheer scale of the Democrats’ triumph in US congressional elections on Tuesday, winning clear majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate, flipping states along the way that had been Republican for generations, will profoundly change the course of the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

Trump is weakened by the decisiveness of the riposte and the instant divisions it has sown in the Republican party, but the new Democratic majorities now face an uphill task in restoring the nation’s democratic health after the president and his Maga movement have had two years to turn federal agencies into political tools.
The outcome in US in particular weakens the extent that one illiberal government can promote others around the world.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s remarkable comeback victory against Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of the Brazilian presidential election, after a stinging loss in the first, won him an unprecedented fourth term with nearly 52% of the vote.

Miguel Lago, a prominent Brazilian political scientist, argued that the result was not primarily about Lula, who had shown the limits of his personal appeal in the first round. “The second round was about Brazilian society saying no to the far right,” he said. “It was a decentralised movement all around the country, and it was not a victory of the left. This was a victory for democracy, in my opinion.”

If he had won, Bolsonaro made clear his priority was to free his father, Jair, from prison, where he was serving 27 years for trying to stage a coup to hold on to power four years ago. The Bolsonaros then planned to take revenge on the judiciary and press ahead with the building of an extreme rightwing authoritarian state.

A second Bolsonaro presidency would have been even more powerful than the first, with a solid, loyal majority in Congress. “A far-right government, but an extremely powerful far-right government,” Lago said.

Like his father, Flávio refused to accept the outcome of the election, but unlike the elder Bolsonaro, he did not attempt to reverse the result by force. Instead, he fled to Miami, where he has continued to insist on his credentials as a national leader.

With one Bolsonaro in exile and the other in prison, Lula has some breathing room – but not much – in the face of a hostile Congress and an array of state governors loyal to the defeated regime. But the immediate threat to Brazil’s democratic institutions has passed, for now.
Not even the students who held the Vučić regime to account with two years of demonstrations quite expected how emphatically their mobilisation of protest would translate into votes on 25 October.
The improvised list of professors, farmers and other political amateurs won 140 of the 250 seats in the national assembly. Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) was a distant second with 103.
The devastating transformation of street power into political power is an earthquake that has been felt around the Balkans and beyond.
Slobodan Markovich, a political science professor at Belgrade University, said the student protest movement of the past two years had had a “snowball effect”.

“Students went to almost every single household, and people began believing that a change was possible,” he said, arguing that belief drew in those who had not previously voted, so very few people had anticipated the size of the anti-regime wave.

There are reports that Vučić had been contemplating a coup if the result had been closer, something his party has denied. But even if true, it is questionable he could have relied on the police to crush the opposition.

“I think there was a huge dissatisfaction among ordinary police officers, and the government had intel that demonstrated that,” Markovich said. “Half an hour after Vučić conceded defeat, the police basically withdrew and in many places they hugged the opposition.”

The new parliamentary majority is said to be the brainiest in the world, if measured by doctorates per head. It will need all its resources to remake the state after such a long period of atrophy under one-party rule.

The result of Israel’s election on 27 October also counted as a win for democracy and its norms, but it comes with a lot of caveats. The coalition led by Netanyahu was reduced from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but the mainstream Jewish opposition bloc only won 48.

The big winners were the Arab Israeli Joint List coalition and the Ra’am party, which won 11 and eight seats respectively, almost doubling the overall representation of Palestinians in the Knesset, and making themselves a force that can no longer be ignored.

The Zionist opposition bloc, led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, has tried its hardest, however, showing great reluctance to enter into a pact that would turn the anti-Netanyahu majority into a government. The uneasy standoff reveals the limits of democratic gains at the election.

“The Arab citizens of Israel are the most democratic people in the region. For years they’ve been the strongest supporters of civil liberties and minority rights,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst.

“[The opposition bloc] looks at this [Netanyahu] government as one that wants to turn Israel into an autocratic theocracy.
