And they fear that it will limit their individual liberties made through hard-won battles over the years for things like gender equality, LGBT, separation of religion and state. Those are things that Israeli Jews think of as democracy.”

Scheindlin said that definition did not encompass the routine violation of Palestinian rights. “They miss out the occupation … That’s not just a stain, it is a fundamental contradiction to anything to do with democratic practice or institutions.”

In an attempt to block off any chance of an arrangement between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties, Netanyahu has sought to delegitimise the latter by launching an inquiry into how they won so many votes, hinting at illegal Qatari funding.

The effort, based on no evidence, has been denounced as an “attempted coup” by some of the Israeli media. Even if it fails, and Eisenkot manages to assemble a minority government, perhaps with Ra’am inside and the Joint List supporting from outside, there are limits to the steps such a coalition could take to refurbish Israeli democracy.

It would seek to repeal some of the legislation passed limiting the independence of the judiciary. It would fire some police chiefs, and perhaps confront the violent settlers of illegal settlers on the West Bank. But the occupation would remain in place, as would the army’s direct control of nearly 70% of Gaza.

Donald Trump told the US electorate to vote as if he was on the ballot on Tuesday, and they did just that. The resulting giant blue sweep mirrored his deep unpopularity. Democrats now have comfortable control of both chambers of Congress, having won big in states that had not elected Democrats in decades.

The vote was driven primarily by domestic economic issues, including the unaffordability of life that the president had dismissed as a “hoax”. The imperial presidency Trump has established was not at the top of voters’ concerns, but it will have to be confronted by the incoming Democratic Congress, if it wants to achieve anything.

The incoming majority is significant but not the two-thirds required to overturn a presidential veto or the 60 Senate votes required to defeat a filibuster. The Democrats could block legislation pushed by the White House, but they cannot count on passing any laws of their own.

They can try to withhold funding, but the Trump White House has a cavalier approach to Congress’s supposed power of the purse. The new majority can hold inquiries, open investigations and subpoena officials to appear before its committee, but those subpoenas can equally be ignored.
Democrats are also likely to find it is as hard as their counterparts in Hungary, Poland and soon Serbia to depoliticise the state apparatus after a period of illiberal rule.

“Through executive orders, flouting of the courts, Department of Justice lawsuits and threats, unilateral tariffs, an undeclared war with Iran, and public humiliation of targeted opponents, Trump has acted like an American pharaoh, often ignoring his own Republican Congress,” said Steven Hill, the author of 10 Steps to Repair American Democracy.
“While the Democrats’ job is clearly to reverse and unwind as much of the past two-year nightmare as possible, in truth it may not be so easy to do.”

articles.title: Briton among six dead after gunman opens fire in Kraków market square
articles.summary: Three more people found dead at home of suspect, who minister says held ‘ultra-nationalistic’ views
body: Six people were killed and 16 wounded after a gunman opened fire in a busy market square in Kraków, authorities said, in what Poland’s defence minister called an “act of terror” on the people of the city.
The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, opened fire with an automatic weapon in the city’s main square at about 3pm on Saturday before being apprehended by police.
He was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views, the Polish interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said at a news conference.
Four women and two men were killed, one of them a British citizen, Polish police said. Three of the victims were Polish women and the remaining two victims had not been identified.
Five foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia were wounded, a Polish government spokesperson said.

Hours after the attack, the prime minister, Donald Tusk, said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect’s close family members – two women and a man – inside his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 90 miles (140km) north-east of Kraków.
The ⁠injured also included two police ⁠officers, one of whom was in a serious condition after being shot three times in the exchange of fire with the alleged attacker.
A total of 13 people were taken to hospital in serious conditions, authorities said. That figure may include the gunman, who underwent surgery after the attack.
It was unclear how many of the injured were shot. Two of them were treated and released within hours of the attack.

Jonathan Balshaw, from Ipswich in England, was outside St Mary’s basilica in the square with his girlfriend when the attack began. “We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down,” he told the BBC.
“A lot of shots were fired, more than 20, with it sounding like multiple different firearms – there were two distinctly different noises.”
Videos posted on social media by witnesses showed people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims.

As it emerged that a British citizen was among the dead, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, paid tribute to the victims of the attack. “I’m shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today,” he said. “My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence.”

A tram driver reported at about 3pm that his vehicle had been shot at by a man in a moving car while passing near the main square, the Kraków municipal transport company said. The window to the tram driver’s cabin was shattered.

The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Police found other weapons and ammunition in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.
The attacker engaged in a “wild ride” around the main square, which is why people were wounded at several locations, Cisło said, adding that the gunman appeared to have acted alone.

The Polish defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, called the shooting an “act of terror” against the people of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, which receives 15 million visitors a year, most of them passing through the main square.
The mayor of Kraków, Łukasz Gibała, said the city would be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Kraków would remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.
“The square will belong to us again,” Gibała said in a video posted on X.
On Saturday evening, the government spokesperson Adam Szłapka wrote on X: “Today’s event in Kraków has shaken all of Poland,” adding that Tusk was “on his way to Kraków”.
The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, wrote on X that authorities would “ensure that the perpetrator of this crime is held fully accountable and severely punished”.
The mayor of Warsaw, Rafał Trzaskowski, announced increased security measures, including road barriers, along main streets in the Polish capital’s old town.
Earlier this year, Euronews reported that the number of legally owned firearms in Poland exceeded 1m for the first time.

Poland issued a record 50,700 gun permits in 2025 and the number of active permits registered in 2025 was almost double the number registered in 2015, according to the police statistics cited in the report.
Sunday and Monday will be a period of national mourning for the victims of the attack.

articles.title: Pope’s visit to Argentina sets up showdown with ‘hyper-capitalist’ Milei
articles.summary: President has opposing views on many issues, and once called Leo’s predecessor the ‘representative of the Evil One’
body: Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.

But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.

“[The government] cut off the supply of medications, special foods and diapers. They haven’t delivered any since last November. The matter is in court,” said the facility’s coordinator, Fernando Montero. The pope and Milei, he said, “have completely opposing ideologies”, arguing that the pope teaches that a person’s worth is not measured by whether they are productive, whereas Milei is a “hyper-capitalist” who believes only “those who compete the most should be rewarded”.

Pope Leo’s three days here – he began a three-country trip through South America in Uruguay on Friday, and will finish with six days in Peru – will be the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987. His predecessor, Pope Francis, who was Argentine, never returned during his papacy.

The trip could prove uncomfortable for Milei. A far-right libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as the symbol of his promised spending cuts, Milei called Francis an “imbecile” and “the representative of the Evil One on Earth” in 2020, and accused him of promoting communism, saying social justice was theft. Milei claims to have apologised when he met Francis in the Vatican in February 2024.

Since taking office the previous December, he has slashed public spending, which the government says was needed to curb inflation. The cost, however, was high. The thinktank Mate estimates that retirees on the minimum pension – 63% of the total – have lost about 30% of their purchasing power. Last Wednesday at the weekly retirees’ march outside Congress, a man held up a cardboard sign reading, “Save us Pope Leo XIV – Milei is killing us.”
Last month, Buenos Aires archbishop Jorge García Cuerva said Leo XIV would find “a divided Argentina and a large number of very poor brothers and sisters.”

But the differences between the pope and the president go beyond typical social issues. In May, Leo XIV called for “disarming” artificial intelligence, while Milei has said he would not regulate AI technology and has instead presented bills to build datacentres across the country and to grant legal status to “no-human corporations”. Federico Sturzenegger, a minister in charge of state cuts, says he has used AI to draft legislation.

Milagros Miceli, a sociologist and computer scientist who leads the Critical AI Lab in Berlin, said the “contradiction” between the two is “pretty evident”. She welcomed Leo’s visit, celebrating how the “powerful figure” of the pope intends to put “human beings at the centre by stripping these technologies of the values that are presented to us as taking precedence over humanity.”

Juan Grabois, a left-wing Peronist deputy and social leader who served in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, said: “The idea of absolute deregulation is at the heart of the president’s agenda, and the replacement of the human element with these forms of algorithmic power has clearly also become a policy priority for the government.”

Disability funding has been a flashpoint between church and state. As Milei has clashed with Congress over a funding law that remains in limbo, Argentina’s conference of bishops wrote to the health minister, Mario Lugones, on 1 April, denouncing “the serious situation facing numerous institutions dedicated to the care and support of people with disabilities in our country”. The ministry has met the bishops twice since, in April and again on 5 October, but without resolving the impasse.

The government is trying to downplay potential tensions. “There’s no way the pope is going to come here to comment on local politics,” Sandra Pettovello, the minister overseeing social policy, said recently. Amnesty International, meanwhile, has written to the pope about Argentina, warning of its “concern about government decisions that affect the exercise of fundamental rights”.

All of this will be top of mind when Milei receives the pope at the airport on Sunday. From the disability home, the pope will go on to Buenos Aires and meet business and union leaders; then on Tuesday he will celebrate Mass at the grounds of FAdeA, the state-owned military aircraft factory in Córdoba, whose workers have protested against Milei’s cuts. Juan Cruz Esquivel, director of Buenos Aires University’s Barometer of Religions and Beliefs, says the itinerary speaks for itself.

“I don’t want to speculate [about what the pope will say], but clearly any mention of defending domestic production, labour, disability or social justice in the pope’s rhetoric naturally clashes with the ideology that Milei’s government has been promoting,” says Esquivel.

Mariano Oberlin, a Catholic priest in an impoverished neighbourhood of Córdoba, expects the clash to play out diplomatically. “Pope Leo has been saying it without confronting, but he keeps upholding the church’s social doctrine as the key axis of his ministry,” Oberlin said. “If Milei wants to use him, he’ll probably have to do a lot of juggling to make him say the opposite of what he’s been saying – and of what he’ll surely say when he comes: that the Gospel invites us to feel like brothers, to respect each person’s deep, inherent dignity, and to fight so that this dignity becomes real in access to rights.”

Since Francis’s tenure, social movements in Latin America have come closer to the Catholic church, and Argentina is no exception. Grabois, who was part of that process, sees the relationship as a two-way exchange. “[Francis] wasn’t the ‘good priest’ who came to help the poor,” he says, arguing that the exchanges helped Francis “develop his social thinking”. “Without the cartoneros (cardboard pickers) and the villeros (people from impoverished neighbourhoods), Francis would not have been Francis.”
To Grabois, the same is true for Leo. “Francis took notice of Leo because he saw him supporting the Peruvian indigenous movement.”

That doesn’t mean all Argentine social movements support the pope. On Saturday, a day before the visit, the LGBTQIA+ community will hold the 35th Pride March in Buenos Aires. María Rachid from the march’s organising committee said: “The church’s dogma regarding our families has not changed at any time, neither under the previous pope nor under this one”, though she notes that Francis’s words on gay rights “brought some relief to many families and their communities”.

But a new development is the rise of evangelical churches, while Catholic identification falls. Buenos Aires University found 57.7% of Argentines identify as Catholic and 17.4% as evangelical, compared with 76.5% and 9% nearly 20 years ago. Last week, Milei inaugurated an evangelical temple in Neuquén and gave a nakedly political speech promising to seek re-election next year. Although Catholicism remains Argentina’s majority religion, it has lost its cultural hegemony and its influence on legislative agenda, Esquivel said.

Nevertheless, a majority of Argentines expect a “message from the pope focused on the social and humanitarian agenda”. Grabois notes the transformative impact that first Francis and now Leo have had “with left-leaning activists” in Argentina. “I’m not speaking about atheists, but outright anticlerical people. People who, 10 years ago, held views that were very, very hostile toward the church,” he said. “I even see them as more fervent [about the visit] than typical churchgoers who attend Sunday Mass.” For Grabois, “in the face of dehumanisation, ordinary people are taking refuge in the only global voice that’s speaking out about this today – which is Francis and Leo’s.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: President urges US for support, saying ‘Ukraine must not be left to face this alone’ as barrage plunges cities into darkness. What we know on day 1,719
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at upcoming talks after an overnight barrage triggered power cuts as temperatures drop. “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners,” the Ukrainian president said. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression.”

Ukraine’s energy ministry said “a massive attack on a number of energy facilities” on Saturday had plunged five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia had throughout the night launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, among which were KN-23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea.

The strikes came before a US-brokered trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi scheduled for next week aimed at reviving stalled diplomatic efforts towards peace. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and US envoys on Tuesday and Wednesday for the first such talks in months. The diplomatic track has been stalled since February when Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran.

Zelenskyy also urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine. “Unfortunately, there is still a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it,” he said.
Related: ‘My biggest fear was being shot down’: how an injured Ukrainian soldier was evacuated by drone

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, on Saturday said he had been targeted by pro-Russian hackers over his backing for Ukraine. Tajani said in a post on X that “backing in a transparent way the freedom and independence of a sovereign state” had made him a target. Tajani said his personal data had been published on the dark web and that the hackers were seeking further information about him and his family and were ‌willing to pay for it.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who has been one of the strongest backers of Ukraine among western leaders, expressed her support for Tajani and said the sale of confidential information relating to public officials was “a matter of serious concern”. Moscow has not commented ‌on the incident. ‌

France’s far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Saturday that settling the Ukraine conflict could not be done by granting territorial concessions without consulting the people concerned. Melenchon, who polls suggest could reach the second round of next year’s presidential election, set out his France Unbowed party’s foreign policy positions at a rally just outside Paris.

Mélenchon has been criticised in the past for questioning the legitimacy of Zelenskyy. But in a campaign speech to thousands of supporters, he said an administration run by his party would take an active role in settling the war in Ukraine. Europe would have to play an active role in peace talks, he said. “We cannot accept that one could consider a peace with territorial concessions in Ukraine without asking the populations concerned if they agree or not to be on one side or other of the border,” he said. “It is for the people themselves to decide what they want,” he added.

A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said on Saturday. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, it said. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

articles.title: Who won New Zealand’s photo-finish election and why special votes could change everything
articles.summary: The shape of the next government will not become clear until special votes are counted and official results are announced on 27 November
body: New Zealand’s right-leaning coalition, led by the National party, hopes to cling on to power based on Saturday’s cliffhanger general election. But the shape of the next government will not become clear until 27 November.
Here’s why the outcome remains unclear and why almost 400,000 yet-to-be-counted special votes could sway the result.

It’s currently too close to call. Neither the National party leader, Christopher Luxon, or Labour’s Chris Hipkins claimed the win on Saturday night. While preliminary results show Labour just ahead on the popular vote – 29.3% to National’s 29.2% – National won more seats in parliament, 42 seats to Labour’s 36, under the mixed member proportionate voting system (MMP).

It looks like 66 seats will be needed for a majority, and it’s not clear yet whether this can be cobbled together by the left or right bloc. We do know seven parties will be in parliament: likely Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori in the left bloc, and National, NZ First and Act on the right.
Depending on what happens next, newcomers Opportunity, who have positioned themselves as centrist, could hold the balance of power.

It’s not typical for the two main parties to both get such low numbers on the same night. On current results, the right bloc could put together a government, but all of the votes have yet to be counted.

The Opportunity party – who on current results have won seven seats in parliament with their 6% party vote, crossing the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament for the first time – could play a big part.
Luxon previously said he wouldn’t talk to Opportunity and its leader Qiulae Wong, but he might have no choice.
Talks can’t begin until 27 November, once all the special votes are counted.

Special votes are those made by people living overseas, or who voted outside their geographical electorate on the day. This year, special votes total just under 400,000, according to the electoral commission.

Special vote results typically skew left. In 2023, Te Pāti Māori gained two more seats than election night results suggested and the Greens gained one. National lost two seats. This election is so close that one or two flipped seats could tilt the balance of power between coalitions.

New Zealand’s parliament is typically made up of 120 seats. Voters gets two votes: for their preferred party, and for the individual candidate in their electorate. There are 71 electorate seats and 49 list seats. The list seats are divided up by parties depending on the proportion of the party votes they win.
Related: New Zealand’s two major parties are flatlining as dispirited voters seek transformational change

The share of the party votes generally must reflect how many seats that party gets in parliament. It’s a little complicated, but if a party wins more electorate seats than party votes, the parliament has to expand to make room. This is known as the overhang.
On Saturday both National and Te Pāti Māori gained more share of the electorates than their party vote, meaning parliament could be 10 or 11 seats bigger.
Not specifically, no, but it can accommodate it. Since MMP’s introduction in 1996, there have been five overhangs, but this will be the biggest parliament in New Zealand’s history.

It’s also the first election where political groups have loudly and specifically asked voters to only give them their electorate vote, to create an overhang. Te Pāti Māori are on track to gain five of seven seats in the Māori electorates with this strategy, while various rightwing groups asked supporters to party vote for current coalition partners Act or NZ First, while backing National electorate MPs. National, who will have five or six overhang seats, warned against this, seemingly to no avail.

Critics say this strategic voting undermines the spirit of MMP, which New Zealanders voted for in the 1990s after a string of skewed results under first past the post system. Two reports since 2012 have proposed abolishing the overhang, but governments of the time chose to ignore them.
It could be December until a final result is known – just in time for Christmas.

articles.title: New Zealand’s two major parties are flatlining as dispirited voters seek transformational change
articles.summary: Voters sent National and Labour a clear message last night – and the parties have no one to blame but themselves
body: New Zealand voters sent the two major parties a clear message last night. They expect more.

In a resounding rejection of the incrementalist political managerialism that has characterised the governments led by the major parties over the past decades, seven in 10 voters passed over Labour, and the same number skipped National. Between them, the two parties took just over half the party vote, 58% on election night. It was the lowest combined major party vote ever.

Instead, a large proportion of the electorate shifted their party vote to the more transformationist minor parties, those with a clearer sense of purpose and vision for the country. Act and the Greens both recorded their best results ever. New Zealand First had its best since 2002. Te Pāti Māori held more seats than expected. Opportunity crossed the 5% threshold for the first time, to win seats in parliament, and may be a kingmaker come 27 November, when the count is finalised.
Related: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’

This was never going to be a definitive outcome or government decided on election night. For months the polls had predicted a razor-thin result that would ultimately depend on the count of the “special votes” cast mostly by people outside their electorate or overseas. That forecast was spot on. As was the prediction that the two major parties would be neck and neck. Labour gained 29.3% of the party votes and National 29.2%.

The major parties have no one to blame for this flatlining but themselves. Not only did their vision and policy offerings fail to fire, but for the past four years, two middle-aged men named Chris (Luxon the leader of National and Hipkins for Labour) have struggled to excite the electorate.

Both parties’ campaign strategies bombed. Luxon and Hipkins spent much of the campaign attacking each other while the real damage to their party numbers came from the minor parties on their own side of the political spectrum. Like the family in Judith Kerr’s The Tiger Who Came to Tea, Luxon and Hipkins held the door open and passively watched their guests raid the pantry.

Neither of the major parties will take comfort from the result. Labour improved by 2.2 points and two seats on 2023, but it was not enough to govern with the left bloc on the night. National fell 8.3 points, and the cost was brutal. Because National won more electorates than its party vote entitled it to, it gets no list seats at all. Senior figures who relied on the list are likely gone including the deputy leader and finance minister Nicola Willis, justice minister Paul Goldsmith, speaker of the house Gerry Brownlee, and high-ranking MP Chris Bishop.

They may have been abandoned by National’s party vote, but in a quirk of the MMP voting system, National was still able to retain more electorate seats than its share of the party vote, causing an overhang and giving the party more seats overall. Parliament normally has 120 seats, and a majority is 61. On election night the size of the house had grown to 131, with six overhang seats for National and five for Te Pāti Māori. That lifts the bar to 66. On election night the coalition cleared it with one seat to spare: National’s 42, plus 25 for ACT and NZ First.

Several hundred thousand special votes are still to be counted. In 2017 and 2023 the specials cost National two seats. This time, with National in overhang, the specials are unlikely to cost National seats directly. But if Act or New Zealand First lose party vote percentage to the left or National loses a close electorate – like Wairarapa where its election night majority was only 139 – its one-seat margin is gone.

Luxon seemed to know it. When he eventually appeared to speak to the nation at midnight, he gave no victory speech, conceding that while National was still the largest party in parliament and had a pathway to forming the next government, the election was too close to call. Serious negotiations and compromises would wait for the final count on 27 November. Until then, the government continues in caretaker mode.

If the count holds, Luxon’s early decision to rule out working with Opportunity will have paid off, by a single seat. Whether by design or by luck, he will have avoided eating his words and calling Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong. But if the specials move even one seat, that call is back on the table.

Nor will a one-seat majority make governing easy. In a tight parliament, every government MP is a kingmaker. One backbencher with a grievance or a leadership grudge can hold the government to ransom. A single member defection could bring it down. So could a byelection, if an electorate MP dies, resigns or is caught in a scandal.
Luxon ruled out one kingmaker. Last night’s result may have handed him 67.
Dr Claire Robinson is a political commentator and author of Promises, Promises: 80 Years of Wooing New Zealand Voters

articles.title: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’
articles.summary: National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time
body: New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.

On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.

But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.

Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.

With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.

Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.

Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.
Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.

“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.

The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high ⁠inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.

Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.

Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
Related: New Zealand heads for election cliffhanger with minor party cast as kingmaker
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.

That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.
The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

articles.title: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.summary: Santiago Peña charged over alleged role in crisis as prosecutors request he be placed in preventive custody
body: Pedro Volpe had just woken up last Tuesday when he saw a message from a friend asking whether his bank account was down too.
It was a day after payday, and Volpe, 50, a writer and lawyer, opened his banking app and panicked: he could not even see his balance.

Volpe was among nearly 3 million Paraguayans, about 60% of the country’s adult population, whose accounts had been frozen overnight. All were customers of Ueno Bank, a digital lender that aggressively expanded across the South American country in recent years, and which, on Monday night, the central bank ordered into resolution over insolvency.

Ueno is at the centre of a political and economic crisis that has brought Paraguay’s banking system to the brink of collapse. On Friday, it led to the impeachment and house arrest of the rightwing president, Santiago Peña.

Peña had resigned the day before in a vain attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who, under the constitution, become senators for life. Lawmakers stripped him of the seat anyway, meaning Peña will face criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.
Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday brought charges against Peña for his alleged role in a banking crisis and requested he be placed in preventive custody.

“The public prosecutor’s office has filed charges against the former president of the Republic, Mr Santiago Peña,” prosecutor Nancy Salomon told a press conference, accusing him of “breach of trust and administration for personal gain.”

In just a few days, he went from being a market favourite among Latin American presidents and one of Donald Trump’s key allies in the region to facing fierce mass protests, being voted out and placed under house arrest.

The now former president is the subject of an investigation by the public prosecutor’s office over alleged favouritism towards Ueno, which, in just a few years since Peña took office in 2023, went from an obscure digital lender to the bank of choice for most Paraguayans.
Related: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis

“It was very easy to use and to open an account,” said Volpe, recalling that everything could be done quickly on a mobile phone. The bank also offered far more generous investment returns than its competitors did.

“Now I’m having to work miracles to pay my bills,” added Volpe. “A lot of people can’t even afford basic everyday things like food; luckily, I still had some money saved elsewhere, but that has only got me this far. I don’t know what I’ll do next week.”

Ueno was so popular – sponsoring the national football team, the league and the country’s biggest football clubs – and served such a large share of the population that businesses have already reported an overall fall in sales of up to 80% this week.
Media outlets belonging to the same financial group as the bank had their operations suspended, including radio stations and the century-old newspaper La Tribuna.

The impact on ordinary Paraguayans was perhaps even wider reaching. The media freeze meant 300 workers had their salaries suspended, initially for 90 days. About 32,000 pensioners whose public pension funds had been invested in the bank were left without payments.

“A lot of people are also not working because they can’t get paid or make payments,” said the historian and political analyst Fabián Chamorro. “Meanwhile, the protests were growing every day, and Peña’s impeachment was the way congress found to prevent a popular explosion.”
A former finance minister and ex-employee of the central bank and the International Monetary Fund, Peña was elected by promising to restore a “great Paraguay” and attract foreign investment.

Soon after taking office at age 44 as the youngest president in Paraguay’s democratic history, he appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, who had until then been Ueno’s chief executive, to lead the central bank. Less than three months later, Spalding authorised Ueno, then a finance company, to become a digital bank.

Peña himself had about $1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.

“During Peña’s administration, Ueno began receiving various benefits, and the government relaxed the rules to allow public funds to be invested in the bank,” said Chamorro. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.

A series of internal central bank reports pointing to irregularities – including loans to companies within the same group – were revealed by local media in recent months but Peña dismissed them as a “false media campaign” against his government.
With the bank having less than half the solvency required to meet its obligations, the central bank ordered it into resolution only after mounting pressure from other banks and opposition lawmakers.

Spalding resigned and, like Peña, was ordered arrested on Friday night. During the week, police had already arrested eight senior executives and directors of Ueno and its controlling group on suspicion of concealing the bank’s deteriorating financial position for months.

The public prosecutor’s office is investigating Peña on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling. He denies all the allegations, and his lawyers said there is no evidence he directed the allocation of pension funds to the bank.
Meanwhile, most affected people still have no access to their own money.

A guarantee fund covers deposits of up to $38,000, which would apply to more than 90% of individual account holders. On Friday, the central bank began making payments to customers with up to $1,565, no outstanding debts and an existing account at another institution.
Paola Benítez, a 25-year-old chef from the capital, Asunción, met all three requirements, but by late Friday afternoon had not yet recovered the money she had been saving for her wedding.
“This has made me a bit anxious, a bit desperate too, because honestly, who am I supposed to go to and ask about this? It’s very strange, very confusing, very sad,” she said.

articles.title: Five European leaders call for closer EU-UK ties ahead of Brussels summit
articles.summary: Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark say cooperation on clean energy will benefit both sides
body: Five European leaders have called for closer ties with Britain ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit.
The leaders of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark, said deeper cooperation on clean energy would benefit both sides in a letter to Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa.

Von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and Costa, who leads the European Council, will meet Andy Burnham on 20 November in Brussels, where they hope to sign deals on food and drink, carbon emissions and youth exchange.

The five countries also want the two sides to speed up work on another strand of negotiations: Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market. “We call on you and the UK to agree during the summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations,” states the letter seen by the Guardian from the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz; the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten; Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever; Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg; and Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen.

Describing the UK as a “close partner in the energy transition”, the leaders said Britain’s integration into the EU’s internal electricity market was “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea area and transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world”.

The UK and nine other European countries signed a pact earlier this year to accelerate the rollout of offshore windfarms in the 2030s and build a power grid in the North Sea. Britain’s exit from the EU’s internal electricity market is seen as cramping the development of North Sea energy and adding to costs.

Bringing Britain into the internal electricity market could be controversial, however, because the UK would be required to make a contribution to the EU budget, specifically to cohesion funds that promote economic development in poorer regions. British officials are wary of a deal in which taxpayers’ money could be used to fund infrastructure projects in central and eastern Europe.
Last year negotiations on Britain’s entry into a €150bn (£125bn) EU defence fund collapsed over a dispute about the size of the UK’s contribution.

In an attempt to head off another row over money, North Sea member states are stressing the potential for the deal to bring about lower and more stable energy prices for British billpayers. “The UK would not simply be paying into EU cohesion funds,” a EU diplomat said. “The UK would be investing in access to a more integrated, secure and competitive European energy market.
“This will lead to more efficient electricity trading, resulting in lower costs for UK consumers.”

According to figures from the industry body Energy UK, published in 2024, if the current energy relationship remains unchanged, Britain could pay extra costs of £10bn from 2024-29, through higher energy bills and lower Treasury revenues.
The industry group argues that Brexit barriers will become more significant over time, frustrating the UK’s potential to realise the full benefits of growth in offshore wind power.

Since he became prime minister, Burnham has said the government would examine the options in the UK’s relationship with the EU, including a customs union, return to the single market or to “go all the way” with full membership.

However, the EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier has said the UK could not rejoin the single market “à la carte”. Speaking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Barnier said: “I said very, very often during these negotiations, the Brexit, there is no cherry picking.
“There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market.”

Labour MPs have supported calls for greater ties. Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, who is campaigning for a de-facto second referendum to be included in the party’s next manifesto said there were “plenty of sensible changes” that could be done in the meantime.

Speaking to the BBC Today’s programme on Saturday, Creasy said: “Our exports are down because we know that it had hit our economy substantially to have left the European Union because you can fight many things in life, but geography really isn’t one of them.
“The biggest trading bloc in the world is on our doorstep, and we walked out of it, which means that we now face a huge amount of friction to trade with them.”
She called recent comments by Burnham, who expressed a desire to form a closer relationship with the EU, as “telling the truth”.

The government further signalled its intention to move closer to the EU on Saturday night after announcing the return of the Erasmus+ scheme, which the UK left under Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal in 2020.
The UK will rejoin the scheme, which allows students and young people to study, train or get work experience in the European Union, in January.
The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said the news was “a clear symbol of our ambition and intent”.

“This time round, we want Erasmus+ to provide every young person, from all backgrounds and all regions, the opportunity to take part and have the enriching, life-altering experience of international exchange,” she said.

articles.title: ‘Life-changing’: parents welcome £10m UK play centre for disabled children
articles.summary: Gympanzees near Bristol will be the first UK site of its type, catering for children unable to use regular playgrounds
body: It has been over a decade since Stephanie Wheen set out to create the UK’s first play and leisure centre specifically designed for disabled children.

Over the past 10 years, she and her team have raised millions of pounds, meticulously researched how to make the centre as inclusive as possible and spent years trialling sessions with disabled children. And soon, the doors to Gympanzees will open for the first time.

“It’s been so long in the making – I try picturing it and it’s just a lot of smiley people. I expect families are going to be quite awestruck because it’s been made for them when they’re so used to there being nothing,” said Wheen.

The idea was born in 2016 out of Wheen’s work as a children’s physiotherapist in Bristol. With her sessions constantly fully booked, she tried to get the disabled children she worked with to do more physical activity in the community so they would not need to rely so heavily on her service.

But it did not work. “Poor access, attitude, equipment that was the wrong size – children’s needs were just not being met in lots of different ways,” Wheen said. “It was completely heartbreaking because these children need exercise more than anyone.”

Research by the charity Scope has found that half of UK playgrounds are not accessible for disabled children, and children with disabilities are twice as likely to be obese than non-disabled children.

Wheen felt a purpose-built activity centre was the only way to address the gap. With a team of volunteers, she began booking Send schools during the holidays to run “pop-up” play and exercise sessions, bringing in three lorries loaded with specialist equipment.

They saw children’s physical and mental health improve instantly. Some walked, held themselves upright or rolled over independently for the first time; others laughed in a way they never had before. Some families travelled up to eight hours to attend the sessions.
“We had a thousand visitors over the first four weeks that we were open,” said Wheen. “Families thought it was amazing, but it was still a pop-up in a school – it wasn’t enough.”

Having proved the idea worked and there was high demand, they started to look for a permanent home – no easy task as a small charity. After years of hunting, they bought a 60-year-old former service station by the Severn Bridge, north-west of Bristol.
They used a loan of £2.2m to buy the 4,000 square metre (43,000 sq ft) site, and have raised over £10m to finish the project. They have £400,000 left to find.

The centre, which took three years to design, will have 10 spaces including a music room, gym, trampoline and climbing area, and dark and light sensory rooms, as well as a fully accessible outdoor play park.

“Playgrounds are notoriously not inclusive,” said Fran Garland, chief operating officer. “You see people sat in wheelchairs watching their siblings or their friends playing on everything, waiting for them to come back.
“So when we went to the designers we said we wanted a playground that was ‘What can I go on first?’ rather than just ‘What can I go on?’”
The two-storey soft play area with a slide is the first of its kind – it has two hoist systems making it fully accessible for wheelchair users.

There will be a party room with DJ equipment that can be controlled by eye-gaze technology. “We’ve got 10- and 12-year-olds who’ve never had a party before because they can’t find something that caters for them so this was really important,” said Garland.
There will be a cafe and a shop selling nappies and feeding tubes, as well as a lending library so parents can try out equipment at home that their child has enjoyed.

Families will be able to book different sessions depending on their child’s needs. Butterfly sessions are for children with complex medical needs, leopard sessions are for those with sensory needs and gorilla sessions are for those who find it challenging to socialise.

Parents with disabled children said the centre would be life-changing. Bethan Campbell-Watkins, whose five-year-old daughter, Malaya, has autism and learning difficulties, said she struggled to take her to play areas and parks.

“Malaya is really active so we would try lots of different groups and just get judged everywhere we go,” she said. “People stare when she’s dysregulated and she’s really upset, saying things like ‘Why can’t you control your child?’ She also has no safety awareness and places often aren’t secure.

“So I’m not exaggerating when I say Gympanzees is life-changing for families like us. I just can’t even imagine pulling up to a place where Malaya can just run in and be safe and we can feel comfortable.”

Kelly Cotter’s son, Adam, 15, is non-verbal and uses a wheelchair. She was able to take him to play areas when he was younger and she could manoeuvre him, but as he grew older, she could no longer manage it.

“We’ve always just tried to give him the best life chances,” she said. “We wanted him to have what every child should have, so we’d try to be creative about where we’d go but our choices became very narrow, and then they didn’t exist.
“So the size of this is just mind-boggling – these kids will finally be able to have a choice about what they want to do. I don’t think I can quite conceive it yet.”
Once it opens in spring, Wheen is expecting the centre to receive up to 200,000 visitors a year.

She wants to open 12 more across the country: “We want every child to be within an hour of Gympanzees. It is unacceptable, really, that this is the situation – what other child has to travel so far just to play?”

articles.title: They have gone 10 weeks without answers. Will these families ever know what happened to loved ones missing after Nepal’s floods?
articles.summary: From Sydney to South Africa, they text loved ones with no reply and respond to questions they can’t answer. But some still hold hope
body: Every day, Nikhila Agastya answers more questions from her two children: has she heard anything about their father? Is he with anyone? Is it snowing in Kathmandu? Is he cold, and does he have warm clothing? Will he come home? The answer is: probably not.
“They know that [their] father is missing,” Nikhila says. “And they are still looking for him. They always wait; every day they wait for him. They won’t give up, they think he will come home.”
Her husband, Gopi Agastya, had travelled from Sydney to Nepal to go on a pilgrimage with the Isha Foundation when a flood hit on 26 August. He did not return home.
It has been 10 weeks since the catastrophic floods wiped away whole villages, reaching settlements as high as 82 metres above the river level.
The number of dead has risen to 1,459. Another 5,285 people are unaccounted for. More than 700 of them are foreigners – including 34 Australians – with families who have had no answers.

Nikhila last spoke to her husband the morning of the floods, before he entered the immigration centre at the border with Tibet. Gopi was excited about coming home – he missed their two girls, aged 13 and seven, and wanted to eat a home-cooked meal with them. The couple planned to take the children on a cruise when he returned.

The days that followed are now a blur to Nikhila. She travelled to India to be with family, while a friend whose husband was also missing went to Nepal and filtered any small pieces of information back: the border was still inaccessible; the Isha Foundation was trying to get in; families were putting up posters of loved ones on hospital walls in a desperate hope they would be found.
Nikhila sent images to Australia’s department of foreign affairs – of the shoes he would be wearing, his jacket, beanie, sun goggles – anything that could help identify him.
“He’s a very lovable person. Everyone likes him. He had good friends. I recently spoke to a friend of his, and he said Gopi is not just his name; Gopi is a brand.”

He was also the sole breadwinner of the family. The pair married 15 years ago and moved to Australia: he worked in IT for a major supermarket chain and she focused on their children. But Nikhila is now looking for work, with a government parenting payment nowhere near what Gopi was earning.
Amid these pressures, she can’t help but hope Gopi might come home.
Every morning for the last 10 weeks, Linda Govender has sent a WhatsApp message to her daughter. And every day, she receives no reply.
Her daughter, Terricia, was in an immigration centre when the floods hit. Now her mother is running a global campaign on behalf of the families of missing foreigners.

“The uncertainty is unbearable,” Govender says from South Africa. “You wake up every morning hoping for news, checking your phone, reading messages and wondering whether today will finally be the day somebody has an answer.”
Govender travelled to the flood zone in the days after, hiring a helicopter with other families to search by air. She returned home to Isipingo Beach, south of Durban, with no answers.

Realising many others were in the same situation, she then set up Global Voices for the Missing – an online community where families can share information and advocate. She says they want Nepal’s government to keep searching to find the whereabouts of the deceased and to maintain regular communication with affected families.
“We understand that difficult decisions have to be made following a natural disaster,” she says. “But families deserve to know that every reasonable avenue has been explored.
“For the families, the disaster does not end. We are still waking up every morning wondering where our loved ones are. We are still waiting for information.”
Soon after the floods, the government of Nepal sought to help speed up that information and set up DNA testing that could match families with the remains of their loved ones.
More than 2,000 people have given their DNA. At the start of October, only 112 bodies were transferred back to families. The process is slow and the backlog is large.
Governments around the world have also been working with their Nepali and Tibetan counterparts to begin the official process of issuing death certificates.

In the days after the floods, families from around the world rushed to Kathmandu. They hired 4WDs to take them as far as they could into the flood zones, they spoke to embassy officials and politicians, they visited the hospitals, sticking images of their loved ones up on the walls.
Related: Two cousins hired a 4WD to find their missing Australian family in Nepal. Then ‘there was no more road’

Last month, Nepal officially ended the search-and-rescue operation, moving into the “search-and-rehabilitation phase”, according to Phanindra Paudel, the chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre.
Authorities would no longer actively search for bodies but would recover any remains, property or other valuables found during the rehabilitation process, he said.
For hundreds of families around the world, waiting for any news, it was a blow.

Those who took it upon themselves to search for loved ones have not found it easy. Nepal’s government is still trying to clear debris to get up to the border with China, with many roads still closed. Nepal has said rebuilding will cost close to US$4.78bn (A$6.93bn) and has called for greater support for that mammoth undertaking, which will take years.
Thousands were displaced – now living in centres, tents, monasteries, or with extended family. They do not know when they will be able to return home.

Sagar Pandey is the chief executive of the Himalayan Glacier Company. His company had 47 people – including 15 Australians – in tour groups in Nepal’s north when the floods hit. His brother was guiding one of them.
“It was scary, it was bad,” Pandey says. “But now, people are trying to overcome; people are trying to continue their lives in a new way.
“It’s been really hard; they can’t forget, but also people don’t have a choice.”

Nepal has been reeling from the floods, which hit during one of the country’s peak tourist times. Adding to the impact is the fact that overseas visitors are no longer coming. Last year, the country welcomed more than 1.1 million visitors, contributing about 6.7% to the gross domestic product (GDP): now, the number has dropped off. Pandey has lost almost 80% of his usual bookings for this time of year.
“We have the missing guides’ children we have to support, to pay for the future for their schools. So we keep continuing.”
Related: ‘How do I not crumble?’ Loved ones of Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods fear others are turning away

Anita Cook is among that small group of visitors returning to Nepal. She owns iNeeta cafe, a world away from the Himalayas, and one of the few shops in the small Australian town of Moyhu, Victoria. She has been to Nepal twice, and is now taking her two boys to hike the Annapurna circuit.

“Once you’ve been there, it just really leaves a really strong impact on you,” she says. “The way these people live, they’ve got nothing, but they’re the happiest people on the earth and they would do anything, anything to help you.”

Her cafe is full of plants she is selling to raise funds, while the local pub is contributing $1 for every parma sold. She is taking $12,000 raised by the small community and putting it straight into the hands of the guides she knows well – they’ve lost families, are connected to the community and she trusts they can give the money to the right people. But she says the best thing she can do is get on a plane and trek.
“[When it happened] I would have jumped on a plane and went straight away. But we are going now, because trekking in the mountains is the bread and butter of all these people.”
For people who went missing at the border, the process has been harder – determining which country they were in when the flood hit has been difficult.
The family of Renee Spry, a woman from the Sunshine Coast, have been waiting while this process happens along with the 49 other families from her group.
“There was some confusion about where they were lost,” Renee’s sister Jacinta says.
“But at the end of it, Nepal agreed that they were on the [Nepali] side, and they would be the ones who would be trying to issue death certificates.”

A fortnight after the flood, Renee’s husband and two daughters travelled to Nepal. They could not get to the border area, but provided DNA samples, put pictures of her up and visited the temples she had gone to before her pilgrimage. They raised the money to travel through GoFundMe and donated $10,000 to the Emergency Action Alliance.
“They were prepared they might go there and not really get any answers,” she says. “I still think it was a therapeutic thing that they did it.”

Jacinta says “it is a funny kind of grief”: to lose someone and have no answers, no physical representation that they are gone. “The uncertainty has probably been the hardest bit,” she says. “Feeling just a bit hopeless about it, feeling removed and a long way away.”
The family want people to keep paying attention to Nepal – on the redevelopment and also the increasing disasters the climate crisis is causing in the small country.
“If you were talking to Renee, she would say there are all these people still trying to live there,” Spry says. “In this ongoing danger, in this evolving climate catastrophe.
“She would be worried about them. She would be like, ‘what’s everyone doing about this?’”
For many families, like Nikhila’s, the lack of information has not extinguished their hope that, one day, their loved ones will be found.
“I always feel like that,” she says. “I just hope, still, something, he might be there, somewhere. I just hope.”

articles.title: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.summary: Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.

Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.

Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.

The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.

The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.

They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.

In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
Related: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Russia has damaged ‘every power plant’ as he seeks Latin American help

Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.

Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”

Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.

Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title: A ‘customer success story’: leaked documents show Cisco doubled down on Israeli military deals during Gaza war
articles.summary: Tech giant leaped to shore up relationship even as company was roiled by worker protest over its role in the war
body: A year into the war in Gaza, the networks of Israel’s military intelligence community were plagued with technical problems. There were major, multi-hour outages to their systems, and repeated crashes. Built-in debugging mechanisms failed.

The problems, which started as intelligence operations were undergoing updates to digital infrastructure, became so persistent as to undermine the “confidence” of Israeli intelligence agencies in one of their top network providers: the multinational tech conglomerate Cisco.

“This series of events happened during the period of war, deeply impacting customer sentiment,” warned a confidential memo drafted by Cisco and obtained by the Guardian. “During a period of national conflict, these repeated outages severely impacted critical operations.”

The September 2025 draft memo was part of a trove of internal documents leaked by Cisco workers furious with the company’s ties to Israel’s military three years into the war, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians.

Cisco, one of the largest tech companies in the world and at one point the single most valuable, is often described as selling the “plumbing” of the internet. It provides the routers, servers and communications systems that move data for companies, governments and militaries around the globe. While its business ties to the Israeli military have received less scrutiny than those of other tech giants, the company has worked with the Israeli security state for years. Israel’s military intelligence contracts alone generated about $67m in business in three years, according to a 2025 document reviewed by the Guardian.
Related: Revealed: Israel demanded Google and Amazon use secret ‘wink’ to sidestep legal orders

While Cisco’s involvement with Israel’s military before and since 2023 has been documented before, the leaked documents obtained by the Guardian reveal the lengths the company went to in order to preserve and expand the relationship as the war in Gaza dragged on. They also show that earlier this year, Splunk – a Cisco subsidiary platform that can process and analyze massive volumes of machine-generated data – made a pitch to join the controversial cloud computing contract between the Israeli government, Google and Amazon known as Project Nimbus.

Cisco pursued these opportunities as the mass killing of civilians in Gaza was amply documented, international organizations and governments began to refer to Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide, and the company itself was roiled by internal turmoil over its own role in the war.

Cisco did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Israeli military wrote in a statement to the Guardian: “The [Israel Defense Forces] is assisted by services provided by a range of companies to meet its ongoing needs and objectives. The IDF does not intend to comment on matters relating to contracts or services provided by other entities.”

Members of Bridge to Humanity, a group of current and former Cisco workers who have objected to the company’s role in the Gaza war, called the company’s work with Israeli intelligence a “shocking and complete contradiction of values Cisco sells to us employees and externally to its customers, investors, and the public”. They said the company, which pitches itself internally and to the public as an ethics-driven company, had become “an instrument of genocide”.

“Cisco has been able to skate under the radar because they sell hardware and software,” the group wrote in a statement to the Guardian, adding that its business with Israeli intelligence made it “no different to an arms company that is supplying the bombs and fighter jets”.
Related: Cisco probably violated Middle Eastern and Muslim employees’ civil rights, US agency finds

Earlier this year, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) found reasonable cause to believe that, following the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on southern Israel, and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Cisco oversaw a hostile work environment rife with racist rhetoric that violated the rights of Palestinian, Arab and Muslim employees. Cisco previously told the Guardian that it disagreed with the EEOC’s findings and that it is committed to being an equal opportunity employer.
The Bridge to Humanity members alleged that the treatment they endured was linked directly to Cisco’s business interests.

“While Cisco leadership was constantly dismissing our concerns about how it was enabling the horrors we were witnessing,” they wrote, “they were behind the scenes going above and beyond to actively continue to expand their business relationship with the Israeli military and ensure they did not lose a cent of business.”
When repeated technical failures presented a “risk to operations” during the war, Israeli intelligence leaders threatened to cancel their business.

In the documents obtained by the Guardian, Cisco referred to its client as the Israel Intelligence Force, or IIF, a body it described as responsible for “delivering critical network infrastructure for various intelligence departments within the Israeli Ministry of Defense”. Several branches of Israel’s government and military are dedicated to intelligence operations, but the IIF appears to be a reference to the IDF’s military intelligence directorate, known as Aman in Israel.
According to Cisco workers familiar with the technical issues, the outages and blackouts endangered intelligence forces’ access to military data.

The leaked documents also reveal that the company activated senior staff in an effort to salvage what it described as a “critical” account, and that it mobilized multiple internal teams over several months to fix the bugs. Cisco also sent staff to meet on site with a secretive Israeli military unit, known as Sapir, which since the 7 October attacks has reportedly been responsible for moving Israel’s intelligence apparatus underground. According to the Cisco documents, fixing the technical issues and training the customer “required site visits by Cisco under extreme security due to ongoing war”.

Cisco’s goal, according to the documents, was to restore “customer confidence” and reverse “negative sentiment”. After fixing the technical issues and helping Sapir return to “business as usual”, between 2024 and the summer of 2025, Cisco noted the client was satisfied and billed the damage control effort as a “customer success story” in an internal presentation.

The leaked documents detail dozens of deals Cisco worked on in 2026 with different Israeli government clients, including the intelligence community, air force and navy, many of which were tagged as “AI” deals. They include evidence that executives for the Cisco-owned Splunk platform sought to join Project Nimbus, though it is not clear whether the deal went through.

Watchdogs that document the private sector’s involvement in Israel’s occupation have found that Cisco has long provided Israel with technological support for its surveillance of Palestinians. Earlier this year, Drop Site News cited Cisco documents which noted that investment in technology had become as important to the military “as the focus on aircrafts, tanks, and any other essential military tools”. It also reported on a company presentation featuring the quote: “Never let a good crisis go to waste.”

Cisco is only the latest tech giant to face the anger of its employees over work with Israel’s military. Since October 2023, tech workers across the sector have denounced what they view as their employers’ complicity in Israeli crimes enabled by the tech products they develop and sell.

“At the same time, we’ve seen more and more reporting coming out showing that a lot of these companies have increased their revenue streams through larger military contracts with the Israeli military,” said Eric Sype, a US-based organizer with the Palestinian digital rights non-profit 7amleh, which has documented several companies’ repressive response to workers’ activism. “The tech sector is moving more and more aggressively into military contracting, and these companies are becoming weapons manufacturing companies.”

Cisco in particular has come under increasing public pressure over its role in the war. A group of investors has called on the company to commission an independent human rights assessment of its business with the Israeli military, and shareholders are expected to vote on a proposal requiring the company to do so at its upcoming general meeting this month.

While Microsoft, Google and Amazon have faced far more scrutiny and backlash over their business with Israel’s military, those companies’ contracts “would mean nothing without the physical hardware and infrastructure that Cisco provides”, Sype said.
“Cisco is at the foundational level facilitating all of these atrocity crimes that are happening and should be talked about and referenced in the same way.”
